questions.explain: The angle of depression equals the angle of elevation from each buoy, so the horizontal distances are 60 ÷ tan 28° = 112.8 m and 60 ÷ tan 41° = 69.0 m. The buoys are 112.8 − 69.0 = 43.8 ≈ 44 m apart. 20 m multiplies by the tangents instead of dividing, 36 m uses sine (the line-of-sight lengths, not the ground distances), 182 m adds the distances as if the buoys were on opposite sides, and 260 m uses tan(41° − 28°).

questions.stem: Two guy wires are anchored at the same point on level ground, 18 m from the base of a vertical mast. One is attached to the mast 32 m up and the other 20 m up. To the nearest tenth of a degree, what is the angle between the two wires?
questions.explain: Each wire makes an angle with the ground of tan⁻¹(height ÷ 18): tan⁻¹(32/18) = 60.6° and tan⁻¹(20/18) = 48.0°. The angle between them is 60.6° − 48.0° = 12.6°. 33.7° takes tan⁻¹ of the height difference, 12 ÷ 18, which is not an angle in either right triangle; 60.6° is the upper wire alone; 29.4° is that wire's angle with the mast; and 108.7° adds the two angles instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: In right triangle ABC, angle C = 90° and angle A = 35°. The altitude from C to the hypotenuse AB is 6. To the nearest tenth, how long is AB?
questions.explain: The altitude splits AB at D. In triangle ACD, AD = 6 ÷ tan 35° = 8.57, and angle B = 55°, so in triangle BCD, DB = 6 ÷ tan 55° = 4.20. AB = 8.57 + 4.20 = 12.8 (the same as 6 ÷ (sin 35° cos 35°)). 2.8 multiplies by sin 35° cos 35° instead of dividing, 10.5 is leg AC = 6 ÷ sin 35°, 17.8 adds the two legs 6 ÷ sin 35° and 6 ÷ sin 55°, and 8.6 is only segment AD.

questions.stem: From a window 20 m above a level street, the angle of elevation to the top of the building opposite is 38° and the angle of depression to its base is 24°. To the nearest tenth of a meter, how tall is the building opposite?
questions.explain: The depression angle fixes the street width: d = 20 ÷ tan 24° = 44.92 m. The part of the building above the window is d tan 38° = 44.92 × 0.7813 = 35.10 m, so the height is 35.10 + 20 = 55.1 m. 35.1 m forgets the 20 m below the window, 27.0 m finds the width as 20 tan 24° instead of 20 ÷ tan 24°, 58.4 m uses the slant distance 20 ÷ sin 24° as the width, and 77.5 m uses 52°, the angle measured from the vertical, in place of 38°.

questions.stem: θ is an acute angle with sin θ = 7/25. What is the exact value of sec θ − tan θ?
questions.explain: The adjacent side is √(25² − 7²) = √576 = 24, so cos θ = 24/25, sec θ = 25/24 and tan θ = 7/24. sec θ − tan θ = 25/24 − 7/24 = 18/24 = 3/4. −3/4 subtracts the other way (tan θ − sec θ), 4/3 adds the two (sec θ + tan θ), 1/7 swaps sine and cosine so that sec θ = 25/7 and tan θ = 24/7, and 18/25 stops at 1 − sin θ without dividing by cos θ.

questions.stem: A chord of a circle of radius 6 cm subtends a central angle of 120°. What is the exact area of the minor segment cut off by the chord (the region between the chord and the arc)?
questions.explain: Sector area = (120/360)π(6²) = 12π. The triangle formed by the two radii and the chord has area ½(6)(6) sin 120° = 18(√3/2) = 9√3. Segment = sector − triangle = 12π − 9√3 cm². 12π − 18√3 forgets the ½ in the triangle area, 24π − 9√3 uses r²θ for the sector without the ½, 12π + 9√3 adds the triangle instead of removing it, and 12π − 9 uses sin 30° = 1/2 in place of sin 120°.

questions.stem: A truck's tires are 30 inches in diameter. The truck travels at 45 mph (1 mile = 5,280 ft). To the nearest tenth, what is the angular speed of each wheel in radians per second?
questions.explain: 45 mph = 45 × 5,280 ÷ 3,600 = 66 ft/s = 792 in/s. The radius is 15 in, so ω = v ÷ r = 792 ÷ 15 = 52.8 rad/s. 26.4 divides by the diameter, 8.4 is the speed in revolutions per second (52.8 ÷ 2π) with the wrong unit, 331.8 multiplies by 2π instead of leaving the answer in radians, and 3,168.0 is the angular speed per minute, not per second.

questions.stem: A belt connects a pulley of radius 10 cm to a pulley of radius 25 cm without slipping. The small pulley turns at 900 rpm. What is the angular speed of the large pulley?
questions.explain: The belt gives both rims the same linear speed, so ω₁r₁ = ω₂r₂ and the large pulley turns at 900 × 10/25 = 360 rpm. In radians per second that is 360 × 2π ÷ 60 = 12π rad/s. 75π uses the ratio upside down (2,250 rpm), 30π is the small pulley's own speed, 6π uses π instead of 2π per revolution, and 720π forgets to divide by 60 s per minute.

questions.stem: A sector of a circle of radius 9 cm has a perimeter of 30 cm. To the nearest tenth of a degree, what is its central angle?
questions.explain: The perimeter is two radii plus the arc: 30 = 2(9) + s, so s = 12 cm. θ = s ÷ r = 12/9 = 1.333 rad, and 1.333 × 180/π = 76.4°. 133.7° subtracts only one radius (arc 21 cm), 191.0° treats the whole 30 cm as the arc, 1.3° leaves the angle in radians, and 267.4° treats 9 cm as the diameter, so r = 4.5 cm and the arc is 21 cm.

questions.stem: A windshield wiper arm is 20 in long from its pivot, and its rubber blade covers the outer 14 in of the arm. The arm sweeps through 110°. To the nearest square inch, what area of glass does the blade wipe?
questions.explain: The blade runs from 6 in to 20 in from the pivot, so it wipes the region between two sectors: (110/360)π(20² − 6²) = (11/36)π(364) = 349 in². 188 in² uses a single sector of radius 14 in, 384 in² uses the full 20 in sector without removing the inner part, 1,144 in² is the whole ring for a full 360°, and 20,020 in² puts 110 straight into ½r²θ as if it were in radians.

questions.stem: What is the exact value of sin(11π/6) · cos(2π/3) − tan(5π/4)?
questions.explain: sin(11π/6) = −1/2 (quadrant IV), cos(2π/3) = −1/2 (quadrant II) and tan(5π/4) = 1 (quadrant III, where tangent is positive). So (−1/2)(−1/2) − 1 = 1/4 − 1 = −3/4. −5/4 makes sin(11π/6) positive, 5/4 makes tan(5π/4) negative, 3/4 makes both of those sign slips, and √3/4 − 1 uses cos(2π/3) = −√3/2, the value of cos(5π/6).

questions.stem: cot θ = 8/15 and sin θ < 0. What is the exact value of sec θ − csc θ?
questions.explain: cot θ > 0 with sin θ < 0 puts θ in quadrant III, where x = −8, y = −15 and r = 17. sec θ = −17/8 and csc θ = −17/15, so sec θ − csc θ = −17/8 + 17/15 = (−255 + 136)/120 = −119/120. 119/120 uses quadrant I signs, −391/120 adds instead of subtracting, 391/120 puts θ in quadrant IV (cos θ > 0), which contradicts cot θ > 0, and 7/17 uses cos θ − sin θ instead of their reciprocals.

questions.stem: What is the exact value of cos(−870°) + sin(1,020°)?
questions.explain: Add or subtract full turns: −870° + 3(360°) = 210°, and 1,020° − 2(360°) = 300°. cos 210° = −√3/2 (quadrant III) and sin 300° = −√3/2 (quadrant IV), so the sum is −√3. 0 gives one of the terms the wrong sign, √3 gives both the wrong sign, −(1 + √3)/2 uses sin 210° = −1/2 in place of cos 210°, and (1 − √3)/2 uses cos 300° = 1/2 in place of sin 300°.

questions.stem: The terminal side of angle θ in standard position lies along the line y = −3x in quadrant II. What is the exact value of sin θ − cos θ?
questions.explain: Take the point (−1, 3) on the line in quadrant II; r = √(1 + 9) = √10. sin θ = 3/√10 and cos θ = −1/√10, so sin θ − cos θ = 4/√10 = 4√10/10 = 2√10/5. −2√10/5 uses the quadrant IV point (1, −3), √10/5 adds instead of subtracting (2/√10), 2/5 uses r = 10 instead of √10, and −√10/5 both uses quadrant IV and adds.

questions.stem: A mass on a spring moves so that its displacement is y = 12 cos(5πt/3) cm, with t in seconds. At what time t > 0 is y = −6 cm for the first time?
questions.explain: Set 12 cos(5πt/3) = −6, so cos(5πt/3) = −1/2. The smallest positive angle with cosine −1/2 is 2π/3, so 5πt/3 = 2π/3 and t = 2/5 = 0.40 s. 0.20 s solves cos = +1/2 (angle π/3), 0.80 s is the second time (angle 4π/3), 0.60 s is when y first reaches −12 (half a period), and 1.20 s is the full period.

questions.stem: What is the maximum value of y = 2 sin(πx/3 + π/2) − 1, and what is the smallest positive x at which it occurs?
questions.explain: The sine is largest (1) when πx/3 + π/2 = π/2 + 2πk, so x = 6k. The smallest positive value is x = 6, and the maximum is 2(1) − 1 = 1. Maximum 3 adds the 1 instead of subtracting it, x = 3/2 solves πx/3 = π/2 and ignores the phase term, maximum 2 is just the amplitude, and x = 3 is half a period, where the curve is at its minimum of −3.

questions.stem: A curve of the form y = a cos(bx) + d has a maximum of 7 at x = 0, and its next minimum is −3 at x = 4. Which equation describes it?
questions.explain: Amplitude = (7 − (−3))/2 = 5 and midline d = (7 + (−3))/2 = 2. Maximum to next minimum is half a period, so the period is 8 and b = 2π/8 = π/4. That gives y = 5 cos(πx/4) + 2. πx/8 treats 4 as a quarter period (period 16), amplitude 10 uses the whole range, − 2 gets the midline sign wrong, and cos(4x) uses the half period itself as b.

questions.stem: In a northern city, the hours of daylight on day t of the year are modeled by D(t) = 12 + 3.5 sin(2π(t − 80)/365). For about how many days of the year does the city get more than 13.75 hours of daylight?
questions.explain: D > 13.75 means 3.5 sin(…) > 1.75, so sin(…) > 1/2. In one cycle that holds for angles between π/6 and 5π/6, which is (4π/6) ÷ 2π = 1/3 of the cycle, and 365 ÷ 3 = 122 days. 61 days counts only from π/6 to π/2, 183 days counts every day with sin > 0, 243 days counts the days below 13.75 h instead, and 91 days takes a quarter of the year.

questions.stem: What are the period and the phase shift of y = 5 cos(πx/2 + π/4) − 3?
questions.explain: Factor out b = π/2: y = 5 cos((π/2)(x + 1/2)) − 3. Period = 2π ÷ (π/2) = 4, and the shift is 1/2 unit to the left. Shift π/4 reads the constant without dividing by b, period 1/4 divides b by 2π instead, shift right ignores the plus sign, and period π uses 2π ÷ 2, dropping the π inside b.

questions.stem: sin A = 3/5 with A in quadrant II, and cos B = 5/13 with B in quadrant IV. What is the exact value of sin(A + B)?
questions.explain: In quadrant II cos A = −4/5; in quadrant IV sin B = −12/13. sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B = (3/5)(5/13) + (−4/5)(−12/13) = 15/65 + 48/65 = 63/65. −33/65 is sin(A − B), 16/65 is cos(A + B), −56/65 is cos(A − B), and −21/65 simply adds sin A and sin B.

questions.stem: cos θ = −5/13 and θ lies in quadrant III. What is the exact value of tan 2θ?
questions.explain: In quadrant III sin θ = −12/13, so tan θ = 12/5. tan 2θ = 2 tan θ ÷ (1 − tan²θ) = (24/5) ÷ (1 − 144/25) = (24/5) ÷ (−119/25) = −120/119. 120/119 loses the sign of 1 − tan²θ, 24/5 is just 2 tan θ, 120/169 is sin 2θ, and −119/169 is cos 2θ.

questions.stem: Using a half-angle identity, what is the exact value of sin 22.5°?
questions.explain: sin(θ/2) = √((1 − cos θ)/2) with θ = 45°: √((1 − √2/2)/2) = √((2 − √2)/4) = √(2 − √2)/2 (positive, since 22.5° is in quadrant I). √(2 + √2)/2 is cos 22.5° (the + sign belongs to cosine), (2 − √2)/4 is sin²22.5° with no square root taken, √2/4 halves sin 45° instead of halving the angle, and (√6 − √2)/4 is sin 15°.

questions.stem: For values where it is defined, (csc θ − sin θ) ÷ cot θ simplifies to
questions.explain: csc θ − sin θ = 1/sin θ − sin θ = (1 − sin²θ)/sin θ = cos²θ/sin θ. Dividing by cot θ = cos θ/sin θ gives (cos²θ/sin θ)(sin θ/cos θ) = cos θ. sin θ swaps the result for its cofunction, sec θ inverts the final fraction, tan θ treats csc θ − sin θ as 1 before dividing (1 ÷ cot θ), and cos θ cot θ is the numerator cos²θ/sin θ alone, with the division by cot θ left out.

questions.stem: If tan θ = 3, what is the value of (2 sin θ − cos θ) ÷ (sin θ + 3 cos θ)?
questions.explain: Divide every term by cos θ: (2 tan θ − 1) ÷ (tan θ + 3) = (6 − 1) ÷ (3 + 3) = 5/6. 6/5 inverts the fraction, −1/10 uses tan θ = 1/3 (taking 3 as cot θ), 7/6 slips the sign in the numerator (2 tan θ + 1), and 5/9 multiplies tan θ by 3 in the denominator instead of adding 3.

questions.stem: Find all solutions of 2sin²x + 3 sin x − 2 = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
questions.explain: Factor: (2 sin x − 1)(sin x + 2) = 0. sin x = −2 is impossible, so sin x = 1/2, giving x = π/6 (quadrant I) and 5π/6 (quadrant II). 7π/6 and 11π/6 come from a sign slip in the factoring (sin x = −1/2), π/6 and 11π/6 use the cosine symmetry, the list of four also takes sin x = −1/2, and π/3 and 2π/3 solve sin x = √3/2.

questions.stem: Find all solutions of sin 2x = cos x for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
questions.explain: Write sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x, so 2 sin x cos x − cos x = 0 and cos x(2 sin x − 1) = 0. cos x = 0 gives π/2 and 3π/2; sin x = 1/2 gives π/6 and 5π/6. π/6 and 5π/6 divides both sides by cos x and loses the roots where cos x = 0, π/2 and 3π/2 keeps only those roots, the list of three misses 3π/2, and π/3, …, 5π/3 solves cos x = 1/2 instead of sin x = 1/2.

questions.stem: How many solutions does 3 tan(2x) + √3 = 0 have for 0 ≤ x < 2π?
questions.explain: tan 2x = −√3/3, so 2x = 5π/6 + kπ and x = 5π/12 + kπ/2. In 0 ≤ x < 2π that gives 5π/12, 11π/12, 17π/12 and 23π/12: four solutions. 2 solves for x on one cycle only and forgets that 2x runs from 0 to 4π, 8 also counts tan 2x = +√3/3, 1 keeps only the first value, and 3 stops at x = 3π/2 and drops 23π/12.

questions.stem: Find all solutions of tan x + cot x = 4 for 0° < x < 90°.
questions.explain: tan x + cot x = (sin²x + cos²x)/(sin x cos x) = 1/(sin x cos x) = 2/sin 2x. So 2/sin 2x = 4, sin 2x = 1/2, 2x = 30° or 150°, and x = 15° or 75°. 15° only misses the second value of 2x, 30° and 150° forget to halve, 30° and 60° solve sin 2x = √3/2, and 45° only assumes tan x = cot x = 2, which no angle satisfies.

questions.stem: Find all solutions of √3 sin x − cos x = 1 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
questions.explain: √3 sin x − cos x = 2 sin(x − π/6), so sin(x − π/6) = 1/2. Then x − π/6 = π/6 or 5π/6, giving x = π/3 or x = π. Check π: √3(0) − (−1) = 1 ✓. π/6 and 5π/6 solve sin x = 1/2 and forget the shift, 0 and 2π/3 use sin(x + π/6), π/3 only misses the second solution, and π/3 and 2π/3 reflect x itself about π/2 instead of reflecting x − π/6.

questions.stem: A ship sails 40 nautical miles on a bearing of 070°, then turns and sails 25 nautical miles on a bearing of 130°. To the nearest tenth of a nautical mile, how far is it from its starting point?
questions.explain: The course changes by 130° − 70° = 60°, so the angle inside the triangle at the turn is 180° − 60° = 120°. d² = 40² + 25² − 2(40)(25) cos 120° = 2,225 + 1,000 = 3,225, so d = 56.8 nmi. 35.0 nmi uses 60° as the included angle, 65.0 nmi adds the legs as if the ship never turned, 47.2 nmi assumes a right angle, and 24.4 nmi takes cos 120 in radian mode.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, B = 112°, b = 30 and c = 18. To the nearest tenth of a degree, what is angle A?
questions.explain: sin C = c sin B ÷ b = 18 sin 112° ÷ 30 = 0.5563, so C = 33.8° (C cannot be obtuse, since B already is). A = 180° − 112° − 33.8° = 34.2°. 33.8° stops at angle C, 68.0° forgets to subtract C, 31.1° drops sin 112° and uses sin C = 18/30, and 146.2° takes the obtuse value of C, which is impossible alongside B = 112°.

questions.stem: A triangular plot has sides of 9 m, 10 m and 17 m. What is its area?
questions.explain: Law of cosines for the angle C between the 9 m and 10 m sides: cos C = (81 + 100 − 289) ÷ 180 = −0.6, so sin C = 0.8 and the area = ½(9)(10)(0.8) = 36 m². (Heron's formula agrees: s = 18, √(18 × 9 × 8 × 1) = √1,296 = 36.) 45 m² treats the 9 m and 10 m sides as perpendicular, 27 m² uses cos C instead of sin C, 1,296 m² forgets the square root in Heron's formula, and 72 m² leaves out the ½.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, A = 40°, a = 7 and b = 10. Two triangles fit these measurements. In the one where angle B is obtuse, what is side c, to the nearest tenth?
questions.explain: sin B = 10 sin 40° ÷ 7 = 0.9183, so B = 66.7° or 113.3°. With B obtuse, C = 180° − 40° − 113.3° = 26.7°, and c = 7 sin 26.7° ÷ sin 40° = 4.9. 10.4 is c in the other triangle (B = 66.7°, C = 73.3°), 10.0 forgets to subtract A when finding C, 6.5 pairs the 40° angle with sides a and b in the law of cosines, and 3.1 drops the ÷ sin 40°.

questions.stem: A parallelogram has sides of 8 cm and 12 cm, and one of its angles is 60°. To the nearest tenth, how long is its longer diagonal?
questions.explain: The longer diagonal is opposite the 120° angle: d² = 8² + 12² − 2(8)(12) cos 120° = 208 + 96 = 304, so d = 17.4 cm. 10.6 cm is the shorter diagonal (opposite 60°, d² = 112), 14.4 cm treats the parallelogram as a rectangle, 20.0 cm adds the sides, and 7.2 cm takes cos 120 in radian mode.

questions.stem: Two lookout posts A and B on a straight shoreline are 500 m apart. A boat C is sighted with angle CAB = 52° and angle CBA = 67°. To the nearest meter, how far is the boat from post A?
questions.explain: Angle C = 180° − 52° − 67° = 61°. AC is opposite angle B, so AC = 500 sin 67° ÷ sin 61° = 526 m. 450 m is BC (opposite the 52° angle), 475 m turns the ratio upside down, 415 m is the boat's perpendicular distance from the shoreline (AC sin 52°), and 584 m divides by sin 52° instead of sin 61°.

questions.stem: From a point P outside a circle of radius 9 cm, tangents touch the circle at A and B. The minor arc AB measures 110°. To the nearest tenth, what is the length of tangent segment PA?
questions.explain: With center O, the central angle AOB = 110°, and OP bisects it, so angle AOP = 55°. The radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent, so in right triangle OAP, PA = 9 tan 55° = 12.9 cm. 6.3 cm uses tan 35°, the angle at P, 15.7 cm is OP = 9 ÷ cos 55°, 24.7 cm uses the full angle at P (70°), and 7.4 cm uses sin 55°.

questions.stem: Chords AB and CD of a circle intersect at E. AE = 6, EB = 8 and CD = 16. What is the shorter of the two segments CE and ED?
questions.explain: Intersecting chords give CE · ED = AE · EB = 48, and CE + ED = 16. So x(16 − x) = 48, x² − 16x + 48 = 0, (x − 4)(x − 12) = 0, and the segments are 4 and 12. 3 divides 48 by 16, 8 assumes E is the midpoint of CD, 12 is the longer segment, and 4√3 = √48 assumes CE = ED.

questions.stem: What is the exact area of a regular octagon with sides of 6 cm?
questions.explain: Each central angle is 45°, so the apothem is a = 3 ÷ tan 22.5° = 3(√2 + 1). Area = ½ × perimeter × apothem = ½(48)(3)(√2 + 1) = 72 + 72√2 cm². (Equivalently, a square of side 6 + 6√2 with four corner triangles of area 9 removed.) 36 + 36√2 leaves out a factor of 2, 108 + 72√2 is the square before the corners are cut off, 144 + 144√2 forgets the ½, and 72 cm² uses tan 45° for the apothem instead of tan 22.5°.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, D is on AB and E is on AC with DE parallel to BC. AD = 4 and DB = 6. Triangle ADE has an area of 12. What is the area of trapezoid DBCE?
questions.explain: Triangles ADE and ABC are similar with ratio AD : AB = 4 : 10. Areas scale with the square: area ABC = 12 × (10/4)² = 75, so the trapezoid is 75 − 12 = 63. 75 is the whole triangle, 18 scales by 6/4 without squaring, 27 squares the ratio DB : AD (6/4) instead of AB : AD, and 30 scales the whole triangle by 10/4 without squaring.

questions.stem: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon measures 24°. What is the sum of its interior angles?
questions.explain: Exterior angles total 360°, so n = 360 ÷ 24 = 15 sides. The interior sum is (n − 2) × 180° = 13 × 180° = 2,340°. 2,700° uses n × 180°, 156° is a single interior angle, 2,520° uses (n − 1) × 180°, and 2,160° uses (n − 3) × 180°, the formula for counting diagonals from one vertex.

questions.stem: A chord 10 cm long subtends a central angle of 100°. To the nearest tenth of a centimeter, what is the radius of the circle?
questions.explain: The perpendicular from the center bisects the chord and the angle, giving a right triangle with opposite side 5 cm and angle 50°: r = 5 ÷ sin 50° = 6.5 cm. 5.1 cm forgets to halve the angle (5 ÷ sin 100°), 13.1 cm forgets to halve the chord, 7.8 cm uses cos 50° instead of sin 50°, and 4.2 cm is 5 ÷ tan 50°, the distance from the center to the chord.

questions.stem: A conical hopper, point down, is 3 m deep with a top radius of 1.2 m. It is filled with grain to a depth of 2 m. To the nearest hundredth, what volume of grain does it hold?
questions.explain: The grain forms a smaller similar cone. Its radius is 1.2 × (2/3) = 0.8 m, so V = (1/3)π(0.8²)(2) = 1.34 m³. 4.52 m³ is the full hopper, 3.02 m³ keeps the 1.2 m top radius at a 2 m depth, 4.02 m³ uses the cylinder formula without the 1/3, and 2.01 m³ scales the full volume by (2/3)², the area factor, instead of (2/3)³.

questions.stem: A storage tank is a cylinder of radius 3 m and height 8 m with a hemispherical cap of the same radius on top. What is the exact volume of the tank?
questions.explain: Cylinder: πr²h = π(9)(8) = 72π. Hemisphere: ½ × (4/3)πr³ = (2/3)π(27) = 18π. Total 90π m³. 108π uses a full sphere (36π), 81π uses (1/3)πr³ = 9π for the cap, 216π puts the diameter 6 into the hemisphere formula (144π), and 42π uses πrh = 24π for the cylinder, forgetting to square r.

questions.stem: A spherical balloon is inflated until its surface area has increased by 44%. By what percent has its volume increased?
questions.explain: Area scales with the square of the radius: k² = 1.44, so k = 1.2. Volume scales with k³ = 1.728, an increase of 72.8%. 44.0% assumes volume grows like area, 66.0% multiplies 44% by 3/2, 107.4% squares the area factor (1.44² = 2.0736), and 20.0% is the increase in the radius.

questions.stem: A steel pipe is 2.0 m long, with an outside diameter of 10 cm and a wall 1.0 cm thick. Steel has a density of 7.8 g/cm³. To the nearest tenth of a kilogram, what is the pipe's mass?
questions.explain: The outer radius is 5 cm and the inner radius is 5 − 1 = 4 cm. Volume of steel = π(5² − 4²)(200) = 1,800π = 5,655 cm³, and mass = 5,655 × 7.8 = 44,108 g = 44.1 kg. 122.5 kg treats the pipe as a solid rod, 23.3 kg takes the wall off the diameter only once (inner radius 4.5 cm), 4.9 kg uses π(5 − 4)², and 176.4 kg uses the diameters (10² − 8²) in place of the radii.

questions.stem: A 1:50 scale model of a fuel tank holds 2.4 L. How much does the real tank hold? (1 m³ = 1,000 L)
questions.explain: Volume scales by the cube of the length ratio: 50³ = 125,000, so the tank holds 2.4 × 125,000 = 300,000 L = 300 m³. 6 m³ scales by 50² = 2,500 (the area factor), 0.12 m³ scales by 50 only, 3,000 m³ divides by 100 instead of 1,000 when converting liters, and 30 m³ takes 50³ as 12,500.

questions.stem: A diameter of a circle has endpoints (−3, 4) and (5, −2). What is the equation of the circle?
questions.explain: The center is the midpoint ((−3 + 5)/2, (4 + (−2))/2) = (1, 1). The diameter is √(8² + 6²) = 10, so r = 5 and r² = 25: (x − 1)² + (y − 1)² = 25. (x + 1)² + (y + 1)² flips the signs of the center, = 100 uses the diameter squared, = 5 writes r instead of r², and center (4, −3) takes half of the differences instead of the midpoint.

questions.stem: What is the exact distance from the point (5, 1) to the line 2x + y = 4?
questions.explain: Write the line as 2x + y − 4 = 0. Distance = |2(5) + 1 − 4| ÷ √(2² + 1²) = 7/√5 = 7√5/5. 7/5 divides by 2² + 1² = 5 without the square root, 7 leaves out the denominator, 3√5 writes the line as 2x + y + 4 = 0 (15/√5), and 11√5/5 drops the constant term (11/√5).

questions.stem: A car speeds up uniformly from 12 m/s to 30 m/s while covering 150 m. What is its acceleration?
questions.explain: With no time given, use v² = u² + 2ad: a = (30² − 12²) ÷ (2 × 150) = (900 − 144) ÷ 300 = 2.52 m/s². 5.04 drops the 2, 3.48 adds the squares instead of subtracting, 1.08 squares the change in speed (18²) instead of subtracting the squares, and 0.06 forgets to square at all.

questions.stem: A stone is dropped from rest off a bridge and hits the water 3.0 s later. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 9.8 m/s², how high is the bridge above the water?
questions.explain: From rest, h = ½gt² = 0.5 × 9.8 × 3.0² = 44.1 m. 88.2 m forgets the ½, 29.4 m is the impact speed gt (in m/s, not a height), 14.7 m forgets to square the time, and 45.0 m uses g = 10 when the question gives 9.8.

questions.stem: A supply package is released from an aircraft flying level at 80 m/s, 490 m above flat ground. Ignoring air resistance (g = 9.8 m/s²), how far ahead of the release point does it land?
questions.explain: The fall time depends only on the height: 490 = ½ × 9.8 × t², so t² = 100 and t = 10 s. The package keeps its 80 m/s horizontally, so it travels 80 × 10 = 800 m. 566 m drops the 2 (t = √50), 4,000 m uses t = 490 ÷ 9.8 = 50 s, 8,000 m uses t = 2 × 490 ÷ 9.8 = 100 s, and 400 m wrongly halves the horizontal distance as if the package slowed down.

questions.stem: A ball is launched at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal over level ground. Ignoring air resistance (g = 9.8 m/s²), how long is it in the air?
questions.explain: Only the vertical component sets the flight time: v_y = 20 sin 30° = 10 m/s, and t = 2v_y ÷ g = 20 ÷ 9.8 = 2.04 s. 1.02 s is just the time to the top, 3.53 s uses cos 30° (the horizontal component), 4.08 s uses the full 20 m/s as if it were vertical, and 1.77 s uses cos 30° and also forgets the 2.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown straight up at 24.5 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 9.8 m/s², what maximum height does it reach above the launch point?
questions.explain: At the top the speed is zero, so h = v² ÷ 2g = 24.5² ÷ 19.6 = 600.25 ÷ 19.6 = 30.6 m. 61.3 m forgets the 2, 122.5 m puts the whole up-and-down flight time (5.0 s) into ½gt², 1.25 m forgets to square the speed, and 30.0 m uses g = 10 instead of the 9.8 given.

questions.stem: A patrol boat sails 30 km due north and then 40 km due east, taking 2.5 h in total. What is the magnitude of its average velocity?
questions.explain: Average velocity uses displacement, the straight line from start to finish: √(30² + 40²) = 50 km, and 50 ÷ 2.5 = 20 km/h. 28 km/h is the average speed (70 km of path ÷ 2.5 h), 4.0 km/h subtracts the legs (10 km ÷ 2.5), 14 km/h averages the two legs before dividing, and 125 km/h multiplies 50 km by 2.5 h.

questions.stem: A driver traveling at 25 m/s sees a hazard. Her reaction time is 0.80 s, and the brakes then decelerate the car uniformly at 5.0 m/s². What is the total distance from seeing the hazard to stopping?
questions.explain: During the reaction time the car still moves at full speed: 25 × 0.80 = 20 m. Braking distance is v² ÷ 2a = 625 ÷ 10 = 62.5 m. Total 20 + 62.5 = 82.5 m. 62.5 m leaves out the reaction distance, 145 m forgets the 2 in the braking formula (20 + 125), 72.5 m uses half the speed during the reaction time, and 20.0 m is the reaction distance alone.

questions.stem: A train starts from rest, accelerates uniformly at 0.50 m/s² for 40 s, then runs at the speed it has reached for another 60 s. How far does it travel in the 100 s?
questions.explain: Stage 1: d = ½at² = 0.5 × 0.50 × 40² = 400 m, and the speed reached is at = 20 m/s. Stage 2: 20 × 60 = 1,200 m. Total 1,600 m. 2,000 m forgets the ½ in stage 1 (800 + 1,200), 1,000 m uses the stage-1 average speed of 10 m/s for the whole 100 s, 1,200 m is stage 2 alone, and 400 m is stage 1 alone.

questions.stem: A car's speed falls at a steady rate from 30 m/s to 10 m/s in 4.0 s. How far does it travel during those 4.0 s?
questions.explain: With constant acceleration, distance = average velocity × time = (30 + 10) ÷ 2 × 4.0 = 80 m. Equivalently a = −5 m/s² and d = 30 × 4 − ½ × 5 × 4² = 120 − 40 = 80 m. 40 m is only the ½at² term, 120 m assumes the car never slowed, 160 m adds the speeds without halving, and 100 m subtracts a × t (20) instead of ½at² (40).

questions.stem: An aircraft flies at an airspeed of 250 km/h on a heading of due north. A steady wind blows from west to east at 60 km/h. What is the aircraft's ground speed?
questions.explain: The two velocities are at right angles, so add them as vectors: √(250² + 60²) = √66,100 = 257 km/h. 310 adds them as if they were in the same direction, 190 subtracts them as if it were a headwind, 243 subtracts the squares under the root (√58,900), and 155 averages the two speeds.

questions.stem: A 10 kg sled sits on frictionless ice. A rope pulls on it with 50 N at 37° above the horizontal. Using sin 37° = 0.60 and cos 37° = 0.80, what is the sled's horizontal acceleration?
questions.explain: Only the horizontal component accelerates the sled along the ice: 50 × cos 37° = 40 N, so a = 40 ÷ 10 = 4.0 m/s². 3.0 uses the sine (the vertical component), 5.0 uses the whole 50 N, 6.25 divides by cos 37° instead of multiplying, and 1.0 subtracts the two components (40 − 30 = 10 N).

questions.stem: A 20 kg crate is pushed across a level floor by a horizontal 120 N force. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.40. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what is the crate's acceleration?
questions.explain: Friction = μmg = 0.40 × 20 × 9.8 = 78.4 N. Net force = 120 − 78.4 = 41.6 N, so a = 41.6 ÷ 20 = 2.08 m/s². 6.00 ignores friction, 5.60 multiplies μ by the mass instead of the weight (friction of 8 N), 9.92 adds friction to the push, and 2.00 uses g = 10 instead of 9.8.

questions.stem: A block slides down a 30° incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.20. Taking g = 9.8 m/s² and cos 30° = 0.866, what is its acceleration down the slope?
questions.explain: Along the slope, a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ) = 9.8 × (0.500 − 0.20 × 0.866) = 9.8 × 0.327 = 3.20 m/s². 4.90 ignores friction, 3.92 uses sin θ in the friction term, 6.60 adds friction instead of subtracting it, and 7.51 swaps sine and cosine in both terms.

questions.stem: A 6.0 kg block on a frictionless table is tied by a light string over a frictionless pulley to a hanging 4.0 kg mass. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what is the tension in the string?
questions.explain: The hanging weight (4.0 × 9.8 = 39.2 N) accelerates both masses: a = 39.2 ÷ 10 = 3.92 m/s². The string is what accelerates the table block, so T = 6.0 × 3.92 = 23.5 N. 39.2 N assumes the tension equals the hanging weight (true only at rest), 15.7 N multiplies the hanging mass by a, 58.8 N is the table block's weight, and 19.6 N simply halves the hanging weight.

questions.stem: A 70 kg technician stands on a bathroom scale in an elevator that is accelerating upward at 2.0 m/s². Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what does the scale read?
questions.explain: The scale pushes up with N, and N − mg = ma, so N = m(g + a) = 70 × 11.8 = 826 N. 686 N is the weight at rest, 546 N subtracts the acceleration (elevator accelerating downward), 140 N is just ma, and 84.3 N converts 826 N back into a mass (826 ÷ 9.8) but keeps the newton label.

questions.stem: A car rounds an unbanked curve of radius 50 m at 15 m/s. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what is the smallest coefficient of static friction that keeps it from sliding?
questions.explain: Friction supplies the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r, so μ = v² ÷ (rg) = 225 ÷ 490 = 0.46. The mass cancels. 0.031 forgets to square the speed, 0.92 doubles the required force, 4.5 is v²/r (the centripetal acceleration) without dividing by g, and 0.23 halves the result.

questions.stem: A 0.50 kg ball on a cord is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 0.80 m at 2.0 revolutions per second. Ignoring gravity, what is the tension in the cord?
questions.explain: Speed v = 2πrf = 2π × 0.80 × 2.0 = 10.05 m/s, and T = mv²/r = 0.50 × 10.05² ÷ 0.80 = 63.2 N. 1.6 N forgets the 2π (v = rf), 6.28 N forgets to square v, 3.95 N treats 2.0 rev/s as a period of 2.0 s, and 40.4 N multiplies by r instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A satellite weighs 9,000 N on Earth's surface. What is the gravitational force on it in an orbit at an altitude of two Earth radii above the surface?
questions.explain: Gravity falls with the square of the distance from Earth's CENTER. Two radii above the surface is three radii from the center, so the force is 9,000 ÷ 3² = 1,000 N. 2,250 N measures from the surface (2²), 3,000 N forgets to square, 4,500 N halves instead, and 9,000 N confuses weight with mass, which doesn't change.

questions.stem: A planet has twice Earth's mass and twice Earth's radius. If g on Earth is 9.8 m/s², what is the acceleration due to gravity at the planet's surface?
questions.explain: g = GM/R², so doubling M multiplies g by 2 and doubling R divides it by 2² = 4: 9.8 × 2 ÷ 4 = 4.9 m/s². 9.8 forgets to square the radius, 2.45 ignores the larger mass, 78.4 multiplies by R² instead of dividing, and 19.6 inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: The spring shown (k = 12 lb/in) stretches under a 30 lb load. It is replaced by two of these springs hooked end to end, and the same 30 lb load is hung from the bottom. How far does the pair stretch in total?
questions.explain: Each spring carries the full 30 lb, so each stretches 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5 in, and end to end the stretches add: 5.0 in (an effective k of 6 lb/in). 2.5 in is one spring, 1.25 in treats them as side by side (parallel, k = 24 lb/in), 360 in multiplies k by the load, and 0.40 in divides k by the load.

questions.stem: A 50 kg crate rests on a level floor. The coefficients of friction are μs = 0.60 and μk = 0.45. A worker pushes horizontally with 250 N. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what is the friction force on the crate?
questions.explain: The maximum static friction is μs mg = 0.60 × 490 = 294 N. The 250 N push is less than that, so the crate stays put and static friction matches the push exactly: 250 N. 294 N is only the limit, not the actual friction, 221 N uses the kinetic coefficient (the crate isn't sliding), 44 N is the difference 294 − 250, and 0 N forgets that friction acts on a crate at rest when it is pushed.

questions.stem: The 200 lb block shown rests on a frictionless 30° ramp. What force parallel to the ramp holds it still, and what is the normal force from the ramp? (sin 30° = 0.500, cos 30° = 0.866)
options: 100 lb along the ramp, 173 lb normal
173 lb along the ramp, 100 lb normal
200 lb along the ramp, 200 lb normal
100 lb along the ramp, 200 lb normal
115 lb along the ramp, 231 lb normal
questions.explain: Along the slope the weight's component is W sin θ = 200 × 0.500 = 100 lb, so that is the holding force. Into the slope it is W cos θ = 200 × 0.866 = 173 lb, which the normal force balances. The second option swaps sine and cosine, the third ignores the angle, the fourth forgets that the normal force is less than the full weight on a slope, and the last divides by cos 30° instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: A roller-coaster car starts from rest at a point 45 m above the ground. Ignoring friction and taking g = 9.8 m/s², how fast is it moving when it passes a point 20 m above the ground?
questions.explain: Only the drop matters: Δh = 45 − 20 = 25 m, and mgΔh = ½mv² gives v = √(2gΔh) = √490 = 22.1 m/s. 29.7 m/s uses the full 45 m, 19.8 m/s uses the 20 m height, 15.7 m/s forgets the 2 (√(gΔh)), and 11.1 m/s puts the ½ on the wrong side (v² = gΔh ÷ 2).

questions.stem: A 30 kg crate is pulled 12 m across a level floor at constant speed by a horizontal rope. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², how much work does the rope do?
questions.explain: At constant speed the rope force equals friction: 0.25 × 30 × 9.8 = 73.5 N. Work = 73.5 × 12 = 882 J. 3,528 J uses the whole weight as the force (as if lifting the crate 12 m), 90 J multiplies μ by the mass instead of the weight, 73.5 J is the force with no distance, and 0 J mistakes constant speed for no work: the rope's work is what friction turns into heat.

questions.stem: A motor raises a 500 kg elevator car 24 m at constant speed in 20 s. The motor is 70% efficient. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what electrical power does the motor draw?
questions.explain: Useful output power = mgh ÷ t = 500 × 9.8 × 24 ÷ 20 = 5,880 W. Input = output ÷ efficiency = 5,880 ÷ 0.70 = 8,400 W = 8.40 kW. 5.88 kW ignores efficiency, 4.12 kW multiplies by 0.70 instead of dividing, 857 W uses the mass instead of the weight and then divides by 0.70, and 600 W uses the mass alone.

questions.stem: A truck speeds up from 20 m/s to 30 m/s. By what percent does its kinetic energy increase?
questions.explain: Kinetic energy goes with speed squared: (30 ÷ 20)² = 2.25, so the energy becomes 2.25 times as large, an increase of 125%. 50% treats energy as proportional to speed, 225% confuses the ratio with the increase, 25% squares the 10 m/s change alone ((10 ÷ 20)²), and 55.6% measures the change against the final energy instead of the starting energy.

questions.stem: A spring with k = 800 N/m is compressed 0.15 m and released, launching a 0.20 kg ball along a frictionless horizontal track. How fast does the ball leave the spring?
questions.explain: Spring energy ½kx² = 0.5 × 800 × 0.15² = 9.0 J becomes ½mv², so v = √(2 × 9.0 ÷ 0.20) = √90 = 9.49 m/s. 24.5 m/s forgets to square x (60 J), 13.4 m/s drops the ½ on the spring energy (18 J), 6.71 m/s drops the ½ on the kinetic energy, and 3.00 m/s sets v² equal to the 9.0 J with no mass at all.

questions.stem: A 1,500 kg car moving at 20 m/s runs into the back of a 2,500 kg truck moving at 10 m/s in the same direction. The two lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?
questions.explain: Momentum is conserved: 1,500 × 20 + 2,500 × 10 = 30,000 + 25,000 = 55,000 kg·m/s, shared by 4,000 kg: 55,000 ÷ 4,000 = 13.75 m/s. 15.0 averages the speeds and ignores the masses, 7.50 counts only the car's momentum, 1.25 treats the vehicles as moving in opposite directions, and 6.25 counts only the truck's momentum.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg cart moving at 6.0 m/s hits a 4.0 kg cart at rest, and they couple together. How much kinetic energy is converted to other forms in the collision?
questions.explain: Momentum: 2.0 × 6.0 = 12 kg·m/s, so the pair moves at 12 ÷ 6.0 = 2.0 m/s. KE before = ½ × 2.0 × 36 = 36 J, KE after = ½ × 6.0 × 2.0² = 12 J, so 24 J is lost to heat, sound and deformation. 12 J is the energy that remains, 36 J assumes everything stops, 0 J wrongly assumes energy is conserved because momentum is, and 9 J uses the average speed of 3.0 m/s for the pair.

questions.stem: A 0.15 kg baseball reaches the bat at 40 m/s and leaves in the opposite direction at 50 m/s. The contact lasts 1.5 ms. What is the average force of the bat on the ball?
questions.explain: Take the outgoing direction as positive: Δv = 50 − (−40) = 90 m/s. Impulse = mΔv = 0.15 × 90 = 13.5 N·s, and F = 13.5 ÷ 0.0015 = 9,000 N. 1,000 N ignores the reversal (50 − 40 = 10 m/s), 13.5 N is the impulse with no division by time, 5,000 N uses only the outgoing speed, and 4,000 N uses only the incoming speed.

questions.stem: A 4.0 kg rifle fires a 10 g bullet at 800 m/s. What is the rifle's recoil speed?
questions.explain: Total momentum stays zero: 0.010 kg × 800 m/s = 8.0 kg·m/s, so the rifle moves back at 8.0 ÷ 4.0 = 2.0 m/s. 20 m/s writes 10 g as 0.10 kg, 0.20 m/s writes it as 0.001 kg, 2,000 m/s uses 10 kg, and 8.0 m/s is the bullet's momentum, not divided by the rifle's mass.

questions.stem: A worker pushes a 60 kg crate up a ramp 5.0 m long to a loading dock 1.5 m high, using a steady 240 N force parallel to the ramp. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what is the ramp's efficiency?
questions.explain: Useful work = mgh = 60 × 9.8 × 1.5 = 882 J. Work put in = F × d = 240 × 5.0 = 1,200 J. Efficiency = 882 ÷ 1,200 = 73.5%. 136% divides the wrong way round (and no machine beats 100%), 30.0% is just h ÷ d, 7.5% uses the mass instead of the weight, and 26.5% is the share of the work lost to friction.

questions.stem: A car's engine delivers 60 kW to the wheels while the car cruises at a constant 25 m/s on a level road. What is the total resistive force (drag plus rolling resistance)?
questions.explain: At constant speed the driving force equals the resistance, and P = Fv, so F = 60,000 ÷ 25 = 2,400 N. 1.5 × 10⁶ N multiplies P by v, 2.4 N leaves the power in kilowatts, 4,800 N doubles the result, and 1,200 N halves it as if P = ½Fv.

questions.stem: In the circuit shown, the battery is 24 V, R1 = 4 Ω, R2 = 12 Ω and R3 = 6 Ω. What current flows through R2?
questions.explain: R2 and R3 in parallel: 12 × 6 ÷ 18 = 4 Ω. Total = 4 + 4 = 8 Ω, so the battery current is 24 ÷ 8 = 3.0 A. The parallel pair has 3.0 × 4 = 12 V across it, so R2 carries 12 ÷ 12 = 1.0 A. 3.0 A is the total current, 2.0 A is the current in R3, 1.5 A splits the total evenly, and 1.09 A treats all three resistors as in series (24 ÷ 22).

questions.stem: In the circuit shown, the battery is 36 V, R1 = 6 Ω, R2 = 10 Ω and R3 = 15 Ω. How much power does R1 dissipate?
questions.explain: R2 ∥ R3 = 10 × 15 ÷ 25 = 6 Ω, so the total is 6 + 6 = 12 Ω and I = 36 ÷ 12 = 3.0 A. All of it flows through R1: P = I²R = 9 × 6 = 54 W. 108 W is the whole circuit's power, 216 W puts the full 36 V across R1 (V²/R), 18 W is R1's voltage (IR = 18 V) mislabeled as power, and 8.09 W treats all three resistors as in series.

questions.stem: In the circuit shown, an 18 V battery drives two resistors in parallel, 9 Ω and 18 Ω. What total power does the battery deliver?
questions.explain: Each branch has the full 18 V across it: 18 ÷ 9 = 2 A and 18 ÷ 18 = 1 A, so the battery supplies 3 A and P = VI = 18 × 3 = 54 W. 12 W treats the resistors as in series (18² ÷ 27), 36 W counts only the 9 Ω branch, 18 W only the 18 Ω branch, and 24 W averages the resistances (18² ÷ 13.5).

questions.stem: A 24 Ω heater element runs on 120 V for 5.0 hours a day for 30 days. Electricity costs $0.15 per kWh. What does it cost to run?
questions.explain: P = V² ÷ R = 14,400 ÷ 24 = 600 W = 0.60 kW. Energy = 0.60 × 5.0 × 30 = 90 kWh, and 90 × $0.15 = $13.50. $0.45 is a single day, $2.70 uses P = IR (which is a voltage, 120), $0.11 uses P = V ÷ R (which is the current, 5 A), and $90.00 forgets to multiply the 90 kWh by the price.

questions.stem: A copper wire has resistance R. A second copper wire is twice as long and has twice the diameter. What is its resistance?
questions.explain: R = ρL ÷ A, and the cross-sectional area goes with diameter squared. Doubling the length doubles R, doubling the diameter makes the area 4 times larger and divides R by 4: 2 ÷ 4 = 1/2, so R/2. R treats area as proportional to diameter, R/4 ignores the extra length, 2R ignores the thicker wire, and 8R multiplies by the area change instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A 9.0 V battery with an internal resistance of 0.50 Ω is connected to a 4.0 Ω lamp. What is the voltage across the lamp?
questions.explain: Total resistance 4.5 Ω, so I = 9.0 ÷ 4.5 = 2.0 A. The internal resistance drops 2.0 × 0.50 = 1.0 V, leaving 9.0 − 1.0 = 8.0 V across the lamp. 9.0 V ignores the internal resistance, 1.0 V is the internal drop itself, 2.0 V is the current in amps, and 10.0 V adds the drop instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: An ideal step-down transformer takes 7,200 V on a 1,500-turn primary and delivers 240 V. When the secondary supplies 30 A, how many turns does the secondary have, and what current flows in the primary?
questions.explain: Voltage follows the turns ratio: Ns = 1,500 × 240 ÷ 7,200 = 50 turns. An ideal transformer conserves power, so 7,200 × Ip = 240 × 30 and Ip = 1.0 A. A step-down transformer steps the current UP on the secondary, so the primary current is the smaller one. 900 A inverts the current ratio, 45,000 turns inverts the turns ratio, and 30 A forgets that the current changes at all.

questions.stem: A straight wire 0.50 m long carries 8.0 A at 30° to a uniform 0.40 T magnetic field. What is the magnetic force on the wire?
questions.explain: F = BIL sin θ = 0.40 × 8.0 × 0.50 × sin 30° = 1.6 × 0.5 = 0.80 N. 1.6 N leaves out sin θ (as if the wire were perpendicular), 1.39 N uses cos 30°, 3.2 N drops the length, and 0.40 N applies the sine twice.

questions.stem: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed quickly toward the end of a coil connected in a closed loop. Which statement about the induced current is correct?
options: Its near end becomes a north pole, repelling the magnet.
Its near end becomes a south pole, attracting the magnet.
It flows only once the magnet stops inside the coil.
Its near end becomes a north pole only if the magnet moves slowly.
None flows, because a magnetic field cannot pass through copper.
questions.explain: Lenz's law: the induced current always opposes the change that causes it. The flux through the coil is increasing, so the coil makes a north pole facing the incoming north pole, pushing back. A south pole would pull the magnet in and create energy from nothing, current flows only while the flux is changing (not once the magnet stops), faster motion gives MORE current not less, and magnetic fields pass through copper freely.

questions.stem: A 200-turn coil sits in a magnetic field. The flux through each turn falls steadily from 0.030 Wb to 0.010 Wb in 0.050 s. What is the average induced emf?
questions.explain: emf = N × ΔΦ ÷ Δt = 200 × (0.030 − 0.010) ÷ 0.050 = 200 × 0.40 = 80 V. 0.40 V forgets the 200 turns, 120 V uses the starting flux instead of the change, 40 V uses the final flux, and 0.20 V multiplies by the time instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A current of 0.75 A flows through a wire for 2.0 minutes. About how many electrons pass a point in the wire? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.explain: Charge Q = It = 0.75 × 120 s = 90 C. Number of electrons = 90 ÷ (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 5.6 × 10²⁰. 9.4 × 10¹⁸ uses 2.0 s instead of 120 s, 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁷ multiplies by e instead of dividing, 90 is the charge in coulombs, and 3.4 × 10²² converts minutes to seconds twice.

questions.stem: Two point charges exert a force F on each other. One charge is doubled and the distance between them is tripled. What is the new force?
questions.explain: F = kq₁q₂ ÷ r². Doubling one charge doubles F, and tripling the distance divides it by 3² = 9, giving 2F/9. 2F/3 forgets to square the distance, 9F/2 inverts the result, F/9 ignores the doubled charge, and 4F/9 doubles both charges instead of one.

questions.stem: In the circuit shown, a 12 V battery drives R1 = 4 Ω and R2 = 8 Ω in series. What are the current and the voltage across R2?
questions.explain: In series the resistances add: 12 Ω, so I = 12 ÷ 12 = 1.0 A everywhere, and V₂ = IR₂ = 1.0 × 8 = 8.0 V. 4.0 V is the drop across R1, 1.5 A and 12 V treat R2 as if it had the whole battery to itself, 3.0 A uses R1 alone, and 6.0 V splits the voltage evenly regardless of resistance.

questions.stem: A radio station broadcasts at 101.5 MHz. Taking the speed of light as 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, what is the wavelength of its signal?
questions.explain: λ = c ÷ f = 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 1.015 × 10⁸ = 2.96 m. 2,960 m reads MHz as kHz (10⁵), 0.338 m divides f by c, 29.6 m treats the frequency as 10.15 MHz, and 3.05 × 10¹⁶ m multiplies c by f.

questions.stem: A ship's sonar pulse returns from the seabed 1.8 s after it is sent. Sound travels at 1,500 m/s in seawater. How deep is the water?
questions.explain: The 1.8 s covers the trip down AND back, so the one-way time is 0.90 s: 1,500 × 0.90 = 1,350 m. 2,700 m forgets to halve, 833 m divides speed by time, 675 m halves twice, and 309 m uses the speed of sound in air (343 m/s) instead of water.

questions.stem: Light in air strikes a block of glass (n = 1.50) at 40° to the normal. Using sin 40° = 0.643, what is the angle of refraction, measured from the normal?
questions.explain: Snell's law: sin r = sin 40° ÷ 1.50 = 0.643 ÷ 1.50 = 0.429, so r = 25.4°. Light bends TOWARD the normal entering a denser medium. 26.7° divides the angle itself by 1.50, 74.6° multiplies by 1.50 (bending the wrong way), 60.0° multiplies the angle by 1.50, and 64.6° is the correct ray measured from the surface instead of the normal.

questions.stem: Red light of wavelength 600 nm in air passes into water (n = 1.33). What are its wavelength and frequency in the water? (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s)
questions.explain: Frequency is set by the source and never changes at a boundary: f = 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 600 × 10⁻⁹ = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. The light slows to c ÷ 1.33, so the wavelength shrinks by the same factor: 600 ÷ 1.33 = 451 nm. 798 nm multiplies by n, and the other options change the frequency by a factor of 1.33 or keep the wavelength fixed.

questions.stem: Which list puts these forms of electromagnetic radiation in order of INCREASING frequency?
options: Microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
Gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, infrared, microwaves
Infrared, microwaves, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
Microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, gamma rays, X-rays
Microwaves, ultraviolet, infrared, X-rays, gamma rays
questions.explain: From low to high frequency (long to short wavelength) the spectrum runs radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays. The second option is the reverse order (increasing wavelength), the third swaps microwaves and infrared, the fourth swaps X-rays and gamma rays, and the fifth swaps infrared and ultraviolet.

questions.stem: A string 0.90 m long is fixed at both ends, and waves travel along it at 180 m/s. What is the frequency of its third harmonic?
questions.explain: For a string fixed at both ends, fₙ = nv ÷ 2L. The fundamental is 180 ÷ 1.8 = 100 Hz, and the third harmonic is 3 × 100 = 300 Hz. 100 Hz is the fundamental, 200 Hz is the second harmonic, 600 Hz forgets the 2 in 2L, and 150 Hz uses the closed-pipe formula 3v ÷ 4L.

questions.stem: A machine's noise level rises from 70 dB to 90 dB. By what factor has the sound intensity increased?
questions.explain: Every 10 dB is a factor of 10 in intensity, so 20 dB is 10 × 10 = 100. 20 reads the decibel change as the multiplier, 2 counts the two 10 dB steps and adds instead of multiplying, 10 treats 20 dB as one step, and 400 squares the 20.

questions.stem: A pendulum has a period of 1.50 s. Its length is made 2.25 times as long. What is its new period?
questions.explain: T = 2π√(L/g), so the period goes with the square root of length: √2.25 = 1.5, and 1.50 × 1.5 = 2.25 s. 3.38 s multiplies by 2.25 directly, 1.00 s divides by 1.5, 0.667 s divides by 2.25, and 7.59 s multiplies by 2.25².

questions.stem: How much heat is needed to warm 2.5 kg of water from 20 °C to 80 °C? (c = 4,186 J/kg·°C)
questions.explain: Q = mcΔT = 2.5 × 4,186 × 60 = 627,900 J ≈ 628 kJ. 837 kJ uses the final temperature (80) as ΔT, 209 kJ uses the starting temperature (20), 628 J treats the 2.5 kg as 2.5 g, and 1,047 kJ adds the temperatures (100) instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: How much heat is needed to turn 0.50 kg of ice at −10 °C into water at 0 °C? (c_ice = 2,100 J/kg·°C, latent heat of fusion = 334,000 J/kg)
questions.explain: Two stages. Warm the ice: 0.50 × 2,100 × 10 = 10,500 J. Melt it: 0.50 × 334,000 = 167,000 J. Total 177,500 J ≈ 178 kJ. 167 kJ is the melting alone, 10.5 kJ the warming alone, 345 kJ forgets to multiply the latent heat by the 0.50 kg, and 188 kJ uses water's specific heat (4,186) for the ice.

questions.stem: 0.40 kg of water at 90 °C is mixed with 0.60 kg of water at 20 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?
questions.explain: Heat lost by the hot water equals heat gained by the cold: 0.40(90 − T) = 0.60(T − 20), so 36 − 0.40T = 0.60T − 12 and T = 48 °C. It is a mass-weighted average, pulled toward the larger cold mass. 55 °C is the plain average, 62 °C swaps the masses, 70 °C is the temperature difference, and 35 °C is half of that difference.

questions.stem: A 0.50 kg block of aluminum (c = 900 J/kg·°C) at 200 °C is dropped into 2.0 kg of water (c = 4,186 J/kg·°C) at 20 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?
questions.explain: Set heat lost = heat gained: T = (0.50 × 900 × 200 + 2.0 × 4,186 × 20) ÷ (0.50 × 900 + 2.0 × 4,186) = 257,440 ÷ 8,822 = 29.2 °C. Water's large heat capacity keeps the change small. 110 °C is the plain average, 56.0 °C ignores the specific heats, 117 °C swaps them, and 51.9 °C ignores the masses.

questions.stem: A steel rail is 25 m long at 0 °C. Steel's coefficient of linear expansion is 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ per °C. How much longer is the rail at 40 °C?
questions.explain: ΔL = αLΔT = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ × 25 × 40 = 0.012 m = 12 mm. 1.2 mm and 120 mm slip a decimal place in the meters to millimeters conversion, 0.30 mm leaves out the 40 °C change, and 0.48 mm leaves out the 25 m length.

questions.stem: Heat conducts through a flat wall. The wall is rebuilt from the same material at twice the thickness, and the temperature difference across it is tripled. How does the rate of heat flow compare with before?
questions.explain: Conduction rate = kAΔT ÷ d. Tripling ΔT multiplies the rate by 3 and doubling d divides it by 2: 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5. 6 multiplies by the thickness instead of dividing, 2/3 inverts the result, 3 ignores the thicker wall, and 3/4 divides by the thickness squared.

questions.stem: A rigid steel tank holds gas at 27 °C and 200 kPa (absolute). The tank is heated to 127 °C. What is the new pressure?
questions.explain: At constant volume, P ∝ absolute temperature. Convert: 27 °C = 300 K and 127 °C = 400 K, so P = 200 × 400 ÷ 300 = 267 kPa. 941 kPa uses Celsius in the ratio (127 ÷ 27), 150 kPa inverts the ratio, 200 kPa forgets that a rigid tank's pressure rises, and 300 kPa adds 100 kPa for 100 degrees.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 2.0 L at 300 K and 1.0 atm. It is compressed to 0.50 L and heated to 450 K. What is its new pressure?
questions.explain: P₂ = P₁ × (V₁ ÷ V₂) × (T₂ ÷ T₁) = 1.0 × 4 × 1.5 = 6.0 atm. 4.0 atm ignores the temperature change, 2.67 atm inverts the temperature ratio, 0.375 atm inverts the volume ratio, and 1.5 atm ignores the compression.

questions.stem: A diver works 25 m below the surface of the sea. Seawater density is 1,025 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s², and atmospheric pressure is 101 kPa. What is the absolute pressure on the diver?
questions.explain: Water pressure = ρgh = 1,025 × 9.8 × 25 = 251,125 Pa ≈ 251 kPa, and absolute pressure adds the atmosphere: 251 + 101 = 352 kPa. 251 kPa is the gauge pressure only, 346 kPa uses fresh-water density (1,000), 127 kPa forgets g (101 + 25.6), and 25.6 kPa forgets both g and the atmosphere.

questions.stem: In the hydraulic press shown, the small piston has an area of 3 in² and the large piston 60 in². A 40 lb force pushes the small piston down 10 in. What force does the large piston exert, and how far does it rise?
questions.explain: Pressure is the same throughout the fluid, so force scales with area: 40 × 60 ÷ 3 = 800 lb. Volume is conserved, so the large piston moves 10 × 3 ÷ 60 = 0.50 in. A force gain is always paid for in distance. 200 in multiplies the distance instead of dividing, 2.0 lb divides the force by the area ratio, and 179 lb with 2.2 in uses √20, as if the areas were diameters.

questions.stem: A block of wood with a density of 650 kg/m³ floats in seawater of density 1,025 kg/m³. What percentage of the block's volume is above the waterline?
questions.explain: A floating object displaces its own weight, so the fraction submerged is ρ_object ÷ ρ_fluid = 650 ÷ 1,025 = 63.4%, leaving 36.6% above. 35.0% uses fresh-water density (1,000), 63.4% is the part below the waterline, 65.0% is the fresh-water submerged fraction, and 57.7% divides the density difference by the wood's density instead of the water's.

questions.stem: A metal part weighs 54 N in air and 34 N when fully submerged in water (density 1,000 kg/m³). What is the density of the metal?
questions.explain: The buoyant force is 54 − 34 = 20 N, which equals the weight of water displaced. Density ratio = weight in air ÷ buoyant force = 54 ÷ 20 = 2.7, so ρ = 2,700 kg/m³. 1,700 uses the submerged weight over the buoyant force (34 ÷ 20), 1,588 divides the two weights (54 ÷ 34), 370 inverts the correct ratio, and 588 divides the buoyant force by the submerged weight.

questions.stem: A 70 kg person stands so that half her weight rests on one shoe heel with a contact area of 1.0 cm². Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what pressure does the heel exert on the floor?
questions.explain: Force = ½ × 70 × 9.8 = 343 N. Area = 1.0 cm² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² (1 cm = 10⁻² m, so square it). P = 343 ÷ 10⁻⁴ = 3.43 × 10⁶ Pa = 3.43 MPa. 6.86 MPa puts all her weight on the heel, 0.343 MPa converts 1 cm² as 10⁻³ m², 34.3 kPa converts it as 10⁻² m² (forgetting to square), and 343 Pa is the force with no division by area.

questions.stem: Water flows at 2.0 m/s through a pipe 6.0 cm in diameter that narrows to 3.0 cm. How fast does the water move in the narrow section?
questions.explain: The volume flow rate Av stays constant, and area goes with diameter squared. Halving the diameter quarters the area, so the speed rises by 4: 2.0 × 4 = 8.0 m/s. 4.0 m/s uses the diameter ratio instead of the area ratio, 0.50 m/s and 1.0 m/s have the water slowing down in the narrow pipe, and 16 m/s cubes the diameter ratio instead of squaring it.

questions.stem: A 1,200 kg car traveling at 20 m/s brakes to a stop in 40 m. What is the average braking force?
questions.explain: The brakes must remove all the kinetic energy: ½ × 1,200 × 20² = 240,000 J, and work = F × d, so F = 240,000 ÷ 40 = 6,000 N. 12,000 N drops the ½, 300 N forgets to square the speed (½ × 1,200 × 20 ÷ 40), 1,500 N uses the average speed (10 m/s) in the kinetic energy, and 240,000 N is the energy in joules, not divided by the distance.

questions.stem: A 3.0 kg object moving east at 4.0 m/s collides with a 2.0 kg object moving north at 3.0 m/s, and they stick together. What is the speed of the combined object?
questions.explain: Momentum is a vector. East: 3.0 × 4.0 = 12 kg·m/s. North: 2.0 × 3.0 = 6 kg·m/s. Total = √(12² + 6²) = √180 = 13.4 kg·m/s, shared by 5.0 kg: 13.4 ÷ 5.0 = 2.68 m/s. 3.60 m/s adds the momenta as if they were in the same direction (18 ÷ 5), 3.50 m/s averages the two speeds, 1.20 m/s subtracts them (6 ÷ 5), and 18.0 m/s is the added momentum not divided by mass.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg toolbox is carried from a shelf 1.5 m above the floor up a ladder to a platform 6.5 m above the floor. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², by how much does its gravitational potential energy increase?
questions.explain: Only the change in height counts: Δh = 6.5 − 1.5 = 5.0 m, and ΔPE = mgΔh = 2.0 × 9.8 × 5.0 = 98 J. 127 J uses the full 6.5 m, 29.4 J uses the 1.5 m shelf height, 10.0 J leaves out g, and 157 J adds the two heights (8.0 m) instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: A 1,500 W hair dryer runs on a 120 V supply. What current does it draw, and what is its resistance?
questions.explain: I = P ÷ V = 1,500 ÷ 120 = 12.5 A, and R = V ÷ I = 120 ÷ 12.5 = 9.6 Ω (check: V² ÷ R = 14,400 ÷ 9.6 = 1,500 W). 1,500 Ω treats the wattage as the resistance, 0.080 A divides V by P (and then R = V ÷ I gives 1,500 Ω), 120 Ω divides P by I, which gives back the voltage, and 0.104 Ω divides I by V.

questions.stem: A boat can move at 4.0 m/s relative to the water. It points straight across a river 120 m wide that flows at 3.0 m/s. How far downstream of its starting point does it reach the far bank?
questions.explain: Only the boat's own 4.0 m/s carries it across, so the crossing takes 120 ÷ 4.0 = 30 s. The current carries it downstream the whole time: 3.0 × 30 = 90 m. 160 m inverts the speed ratio (120 × 4.0 ÷ 3.0), 72 m times the crossing with the 5.0 m/s resultant speed (120 ÷ 5.0 = 24 s), 150 m is the total length of the slanted path (5.0 × 30), and 40 m divides the width by the current speed.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from the top of a cliff 44.1 m above the sea. Ignoring air resistance (g = 9.8 m/s²), how fast is it moving when it hits the water?
questions.explain: Fall time: t = √(2h/g) = √(88.2 ÷ 9.8) = 3.0 s, so the vertical speed is 9.8 × 3.0 = 29.4 m/s. The horizontal 15 m/s is unchanged, so the speed is √(15² + 29.4²) = √1,089 = 33.0 m/s. 44.4 m/s adds the components as plain numbers, 29.4 m/s is the vertical part alone, 25.6 m/s uses v² = gh and loses the 2, and 46.6 m/s combines the 15 m/s with the 44.1 m height as if it were a speed.

questions.stem: A shell is fired at 25 m/s at 53° above level ground. Using sin 53° = 0.80, cos 53° = 0.60 and g = 9.8 m/s², and ignoring air resistance, how far away does it land?
questions.explain: Components: vx = 25 × 0.60 = 15 m/s and vy = 25 × 0.80 = 20 m/s. Time of flight = 2vy ÷ g = 40 ÷ 9.8 = 4.08 s, so the range is 15 × 4.08 = 61.2 m. 30.6 m uses only the time to the top of the arc, 20.4 m is the maximum height (vy² ÷ 2g), 122 m doubles the flight time twice, and 63.8 m is v² ÷ g, the range at 45°, which ignores the actual angle.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown straight up at 14.7 m/s from the edge of a roof 49 m above the ground, and it falls past the roof to the ground. Taking g = 9.8 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, how long after the throw does it hit the ground?
questions.explain: Take up as positive: −49 = 14.7t − 4.9t², so 4.9t² − 14.7t − 49 = 0 and t² − 3t − 10 = 0. (t − 5)(t + 2) = 0, so t = 5.0 s. 3.2 s is the time to drop 49 m from rest, ignoring the upward throw, 3.0 s is when the ball passes the roof again (2 × 14.7 ÷ 9.8), 2.0 s is the size of the negative root, and 3.5 s is only the fall from the top of the flight (61 m), leaving out the 1.5 s rise.

questions.stem: A patrol boat takes 4.0 h to travel 60 km upstream and 2.0 h to make the same trip back downstream. What are the boat's speed in still water and the speed of the current?
questions.explain: Upstream ground speed = 60 ÷ 4.0 = 15 km/h = b − c, and downstream = 60 ÷ 2.0 = 30 km/h = b + c. Adding: 2b = 45, so b = 22.5 km/h, and c = 30 − 22.5 = 7.5 km/h. 15.0 and 30.0 km/h are the two ground speeds, 45.0 and 15.0 km/h are the sum and difference without halving, 22.5 and 15.0 km/h halve only the sum, and 7.5 and 22.5 km/h swap the boat and the current.

questions.stem: A cart's velocity rises uniformly from 0 to 12 m/s in 4.0 s, stays at 12 m/s for 6.0 s, then falls uniformly to 0 in 3.0 s. What is its average speed over the 13 s?
questions.explain: Distance is the area under the velocity-time graph: ½ × 4.0 × 12 + 6.0 × 12 + ½ × 3.0 × 12 = 24 + 72 + 18 = 114 m. Average speed = 114 ÷ 13 = 8.77 m/s. 6.00 m/s averages the start and top speeds, 5.54 m/s counts only the 72 m at constant speed, 11.4 m/s divides by 10 s and drops the braking time, and 8.00 m/s averages the three segment speeds (6, 12 and 6) without weighting them by time.

questions.stem: A stone dropped from rest falls 34.3 m during the last 1.0 s before it hits the ground. Taking g = 9.8 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, from what height was it dropped?
questions.explain: If the fall lasts t seconds, the last second covers 4.9t² − 4.9(t − 1)² = 9.8t − 4.9 = 34.3, so t = 4.0 s. Height = 4.9 × 4.0² = 78.4 m. 60.0 m treats 34.3 as the impact speed (34.3² ÷ 19.6), 34.3 m is only the last second, 44.1 m is the distance fallen in the first 3.0 s, and 157 m drops the ½ in ½gt².

questions.stem: With its wheels locked, a car traveling at 15 m/s skids to a stop in 18 m. With the same deceleration, how far would it skid from 25 m/s?
questions.explain: From v² = 2ad, stopping distance is proportional to v². Distance = 18 × (25 ÷ 15)² = 18 × 2.78 = 50 m. 30 m scales linearly with speed, 32 m is only the extra distance (625 − 225) ÷ (2 × 6.25), 83 m cubes the speed ratio, and 6.5 m squares the ratio upside down.

questions.stem: A ball is kicked at 18 m/s at 30° above the horizontal toward a vertical wall 22 m away. Ignoring air resistance (g = 9.8 m/s²), how far above the kick point does it hit the wall?
questions.explain: vx = 18 cos 30° = 15.6 m/s and vy = 18 sin 30° = 9.0 m/s. The ball reaches the wall at t = 22 ÷ 15.6 = 1.41 s, when y = 9.0 × 1.41 − 4.9 × 1.41² = 12.7 − 9.8 = 2.9 m. 12.7 m ignores gravity, 8.8 m swaps sine and cosine, 6.8 m drops the ½ in ½gt² (and really puts the ball 6.8 m below the kick point), and 3.7 m finds the time with the full 18 m/s instead of its horizontal part.

questions.stem: A ship sails 50 km on a bearing of 060° and then 30 km due south. Using sin 60° = 0.866 and cos 60° = 0.500, how far is it from its starting point?
questions.explain: First leg: east 50 × 0.866 = 43.3 km and north 50 × 0.500 = 25.0 km. After 30 km south the north component is 25.0 − 30 = −5.0 km. Distance = √(43.3² + 5.0²) = 43.6 km. 80.0 km adds the distances, 20.0 km subtracts them, 58.3 km treats the legs as perpendicular (√(50² + 30²)), and 70.0 km uses the law of cosines with the 120° change of heading instead of the 60° angle inside the triangle.

questions.stem: A 12 kg box is pulled up a 37° incline at constant speed by a rope parallel to the slope. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. Using sin 37° = 0.60, cos 37° = 0.80 and g = 9.8 m/s², what is the tension in the rope?
questions.explain: Weight = 12 × 9.8 = 117.6 N. Down-slope component = 117.6 × 0.60 = 70.6 N; normal force = 117.6 × 0.80 = 94.1 N, so friction = 0.25 × 94.1 = 23.5 N, also down the slope while the box moves up. Constant speed means T = 70.6 + 23.5 = 94.1 N. 47.0 N subtracts the friction, 70.6 N leaves friction out, 88.2 N works out friction from sin 37° instead of cos 37°, and 9.60 N uses the mass instead of the weight.

questions.stem: Masses of 5.0 kg and 3.0 kg hang on either side of a light string over a frictionless pulley. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what are the acceleration of the masses and the tension in the string?
questions.explain: Net force = (5.0 − 3.0) × 9.8 = 19.6 N acting on 8.0 kg, so a = 2.45 m/s². For the rising 3.0 kg mass, T − 29.4 = 3.0 × 2.45, so T = 36.8 N. 29.4 N and 49.0 N are the two weights (true only at rest), 3.92 m/s² divides the net force by the 5.0 kg mass alone, and 39.2 N averages the two weights.

questions.stem: A curve of radius 80 m is banked so that a car taking it at 20 m/s needs no friction. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what is the bank angle, to the nearest tenth of a degree?
questions.explain: With no friction, the horizontal part of the normal force supplies the centripetal force and the vertical part balances the weight, so tan θ = v² ÷ (rg) = 400 ÷ 784 = 0.510 and θ = 27.0°. 63.0° is the complement (the ratio inverted), 30.7° takes the inverse sine instead of the inverse tangent, 78.7° leaves out g (tan θ = 400 ÷ 80), and 14.3° puts a stray 2 in the denominator.

questions.stem: A 0.20 kg ball on a string is swung in a vertical circle of radius 0.60 m. At the top of the circle it moves at 4.0 m/s. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what is the tension in the string at that point?
questions.explain: At the top, tension and weight both point down toward the center: T + mg = mv² ÷ r. mv² ÷ r = 0.20 × 16 ÷ 0.60 = 5.33 N and mg = 1.96 N, so T = 5.33 − 1.96 = 3.37 N. 7.29 N adds the weight, which is the bottom-of-the-circle formula, 5.33 N ignores the weight, 0.71 N uses the 1.20 m diameter as the radius, and 1.96 N is the weight alone.

questions.stem: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at an altitude equal to one Earth radius. Taking Earth's radius as 6.4 × 10⁶ m and g at the surface as 9.8 m/s², what is its orbital period, in hours?
questions.explain: The orbit radius is r = 2R, where gravity is g ÷ 4. Setting g(R/r)² = 4π²r ÷ T² gives T = 2π√(r³ ÷ gR²) = 2π√(8R ÷ g) = 2π × 2,286 s = 14,360 s = 3.99 h. 1.41 h ignores the altitude (r = R), 1.99 h uses r = 2R but keeps surface gravity, 2.82 h squares the orbit radius instead of cubing it, and 0.635 h leaves out the 2π.

questions.stem: A uniform beam 4.0 m long weighing 200 N rests on supports at its two ends. A 600 N load sits 1.0 m from the left end. What upward force does the left support exert?
questions.explain: Take torques about the right support: F_left × 4.0 = 200 × 2.0 + 600 × 3.0 = 2,200 N·m, so F_left = 550 N (and the right support carries 800 − 550 = 250 N). 250 N is the right support's force, 450 N ignores the beam's own weight, 400 N splits the 800 N total evenly, and 150 N measures the load's lever arm from the wrong end and drops the beam weight.

questions.stem: A uniform horizontal boom 3.0 m long weighing 400 N is hinged to a wall. A 600 N sign hangs from its outer end, which is held by a cable running back to the wall at 30° to the boom. What is the tension in the cable? (sin 30° = 0.500, cos 30° = 0.866)
questions.explain: Torques about the hinge: the cable's perpendicular part T sin 30° acts 3.0 m out, the boom weight acts at its 1.5 m midpoint and the sign at 3.0 m. T × 0.500 × 3.0 = 400 × 1.5 + 600 × 3.0 = 2,400, so T = 1,600 N. 1,200 N leaves out the boom's weight, 924 N uses cos 30° instead of sin 30°, 800 N ignores the cable angle, and 2,000 N puts the boom's weight at its far end.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg mass hung from a vertical spring stretches it 4.0 cm. The mass is then pulled down and released. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what is the period of its oscillation?
questions.explain: Spring constant: k = mg ÷ x = 19.6 ÷ 0.040 = 490 N/m. Period: T = 2π√(m ÷ k) = 2π√(2.0 ÷ 490) = 0.401 s. 4.01 s leaves the stretch in centimeters (k = 4.9), 1.26 s uses the mass instead of the weight to find k, 0.0639 s leaves out the 2π, and 98.3 s inverts the ratio under the root.

questions.stem: A 25 kg crate rests on a ramp tilted at 20°. The coefficient of static friction is 0.40. Using sin 20° = 0.342, cos 20° = 0.940 and g = 9.8 m/s², what is the friction force on the crate?
questions.explain: Check sliding first: the down-slope pull is 245 × 0.342 = 83.8 N, while static friction can supply up to 0.40 × 245 × 0.940 = 92.1 N. The crate stays put, so friction only needs to match the pull: 83.8 N. 92.1 N is the maximum possible, not the actual, friction, 230 N is the normal force, 98.0 N takes μ times the full weight, and 0 N wrongly assumes friction acts only when something slides.

questions.stem: An 80 kg sailor stands on a scale in an elevator that is moving down at 6.0 m/s and slows uniformly to a stop in 3.0 s. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what does the scale read while it slows?
questions.explain: Slowing a downward motion means the acceleration points up: a = 6.0 ÷ 3.0 = 2.0 m/s² upward. N − mg = ma, so N = 80 × (9.8 + 2.0) = 944 N. 624 N takes the acceleration as downward because the elevator moves down, 784 N is the sailor's weight, 160 N is only ma, and 1,264 N uses the 6.0 m/s speed as the acceleration.

questions.stem: A 5.0 kg block starts from rest at the top of a ramp 6.0 m long inclined at 30°. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.20. Taking g = 9.8 m/s² and cos 30° = 0.866, how fast is the block moving at the bottom?
questions.explain: Height lost = 6.0 × sin 30° = 3.0 m, releasing 5.0 × 9.8 × 3.0 = 147 J. Friction = 0.20 × 49 × 0.866 = 8.49 N, which does 8.49 × 6.0 = 50.9 J of work. KE = 147 − 50.9 = 96.1 J, so v = √(2 × 96.1 ÷ 5.0) = 6.20 m/s. 7.67 m/s ignores friction, 5.94 m/s finds friction from the full weight instead of the normal force, 9.86 m/s uses the 6.0 m ramp length as the height, and 4.38 m/s drops the 2 in v = √(2KE ÷ m).

questions.stem: A 20 g bullet embeds itself in a 2.0 kg wooden block hanging from strings, and the block swings up 0.20 m. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what was the bullet's speed?
questions.explain: After the collision energy is conserved: v = √(2gh) = √3.92 = 1.98 m/s for block plus bullet. During the collision only momentum is conserved: 0.020 × v_b = 2.02 × 1.98, so v_b = 200 m/s. 19.9 m/s wrongly conserves kinetic energy through the collision, 141 m/s leaves the 2 out of √(2gh) (√(gh) = 1.40 m/s after impact), 396 m/s skips the square root (uses 2gh as the speed), and 1.98 m/s is the block's speed after impact.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg cart moving at 6.0 m/s collides head-on with a 4.0 kg cart at rest. The collision is perfectly elastic. What are the velocities of the 2.0 kg cart and the 4.0 kg cart just afterward?
questions.explain: For an elastic collision with the target at rest: v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u ÷ (m₁ + m₂) = (−2.0 ÷ 6.0) × 6.0 = −2.0 m/s, and v₂ = 2m₁u ÷ (m₁ + m₂) = 4.0 ÷ 6.0 × 6.0 = 4.0 m/s. Check: momentum 12 = −4 + 16 and KE 36 J = 4 + 32 J. Stopping the first cart conserves momentum but loses kinetic energy, 2.0 m/s together is the perfectly inelastic result, bouncing back at 6.0 m/s treats the 4.0 kg cart as a fixed wall, and the last choice swaps the masses in the formulas.

questions.stem: A 1,500 kg truck climbs a road that rises 1 m for every 20 m traveled along it, at a constant 15 m/s, against 800 N of air and rolling resistance. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what power does the engine deliver?
questions.explain: Gravity's component along the road is mg × (1 ÷ 20) = 14,700 ÷ 20 = 735 N. At constant speed the drive force is 735 + 800 = 1,535 N, so P = Fv = 1,535 × 15 = 23,000 W = 23.0 kW. 11.0 kW ignores the resistance, 12.0 kW ignores the slope, 13.1 kW uses the mass (75) instead of the weight component (735), and 233 kW pushes against the full weight as if lifting the truck vertically.

questions.stem: A 0.40 kg ball moving east at 10 m/s is struck by a force that averages 120 N west for 0.050 s. What is the ball's velocity afterward?
questions.explain: Impulse = 120 × 0.050 = 6.0 N·s west. Taking east as positive, p = 0.40 × 10 − 6.0 = 4.0 − 6.0 = −2.0 kg·m/s, so v = −2.0 ÷ 0.40 = 5.0 m/s west. 25.0 m/s east adds the impulse in the wrong direction, 15.0 m/s west is only the change in velocity, 4.0 m/s east subtracts the impulse straight from the speed without dividing by the mass, and 2.0 m/s west stops at the final momentum.

questions.stem: A 4.0 kg object at rest breaks into three pieces. A 1.0 kg piece flies east at 12 m/s and another 1.0 kg piece flies north at 9.0 m/s. What is the speed of the remaining 2.0 kg piece?
questions.explain: Total momentum stays zero, so the third piece carries momentum equal and opposite to the vector sum of the other two: √(12² + 9.0²) = 15 kg·m/s. Its speed is 15 ÷ 2.0 = 7.50 m/s. 15.0 m/s forgets to divide by the mass, 10.5 m/s adds the momenta as plain numbers (21 ÷ 2), 1.50 m/s subtracts them (3 ÷ 2), and 3.75 m/s divides by the whole 4.0 kg.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg block sliding at 4.0 m/s crosses a rough patch 1.5 m long (coefficient of kinetic friction 0.20) and then runs into a spring with k = 800 N/m on a frictionless surface. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what is the spring's maximum compression?
questions.explain: Starting KE = ½ × 2.0 × 4.0² = 16.0 J. Friction removes 0.20 × 2.0 × 9.8 × 1.5 = 5.88 J, leaving 10.12 J. Then ½kx² = 10.12 gives x = √(20.24 ÷ 800) = 0.159 m. 0.200 m ignores the rough patch, 0.112 m drops the ½ in the spring energy, 0.256 m drops the ½ in the kinetic energy, and 0.234 m adds the friction work instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: A pump lifts 300 L of water per minute through a height of 12 m. One liter of water has a mass of 1.0 kg, and the pump is 75% efficient. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what electrical power does the pump draw?
questions.explain: Useful power = mgh ÷ t = 300 × 9.8 × 12 ÷ 60 s = 588 W. The input must be larger: 588 ÷ 0.75 = 784 W. 588 W is the useful output only, 441 W multiplies by the efficiency instead of dividing, 80 W uses the mass instead of the weight, and 47.0 kW treats 300 L per minute as 300 L per second.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg object and an 8.0 kg object have equal momentum. The 2.0 kg object has 64 J of kinetic energy. What is the kinetic energy of the 8.0 kg object?
questions.explain: Kinetic energy can be written KE = p² ÷ 2m. With p the same, KE is inversely proportional to the mass, so the 8.0 kg object has 64 × (2.0 ÷ 8.0) = 16 J. (Check: the 2.0 kg object moves at 8.0 m/s, so p = 16 and the 8.0 kg object moves at 2.0 m/s.) 256 J multiplies by the mass ratio, 64 J assumes equal momentum means equal energy, 32 J halves the energy, and 4.0 J squares the mass ratio.

questions.stem: A 2,200 μF capacitor is charged to 50 V and then connected across a 10 Ω resistor. How much energy was stored, and what current flows the instant the connection is made?
questions.explain: Energy: ½CV² = ½ × 2.2 × 10⁻³ × 50² = 2.75 J. At the first instant the full 50 V is across the resistor, so I = 50 ÷ 10 = 5.0 A. 5.50 J drops the ½, 0.0550 J forgets to square the voltage, 500 A multiplies V by R, and 2,750 J reads μF as mF.

questions.stem: A 6.0 μF capacitor and a 3.0 μF capacitor are connected in series across a 12 V supply. What is the charge on each capacitor, and the voltage across the 3.0 μF capacitor?
questions.explain: In series, 1/C = 1/6.0 + 1/3.0 = 1/2.0, so C = 2.0 μF and Q = 2.0 × 12 = 24 μC on each capacitor. The smaller capacitor takes the larger voltage: V = Q ÷ C = 24 ÷ 3.0 = 8.0 V (the 6.0 μF has 4.0 V). 108 μC adds the capacitances as if in parallel, 4.0 V is the voltage across the 6.0 μF, 36 μC puts the whole 12 V across the 3.0 μF capacitor, and 48 μC multiplies the 6.0 μF by the 3.0 μF capacitor's voltage.

questions.stem: A copper wire is 50 m long with a diameter of 1.0 mm. Copper's resistivity is 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m. What is the wire's resistance?
questions.explain: Cross-section: A = πr² = π × (0.50 × 10⁻³)² = 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m². R = ρL ÷ A = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ × 50 ÷ 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.08 Ω. 0.271 Ω uses the diameter as the radius, 3.40 Ω forgets the π, 0.850 Ω takes the area as d², and 1.08 × 10⁻⁶ Ω leaves the radius in millimeters.

questions.stem: A 24 V battery drives a 6.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of resistors, 12 Ω and 6.0 Ω. How much power does the 12 Ω resistor dissipate?
questions.explain: The parallel pair is 12 × 6.0 ÷ 18 = 4.0 Ω, so the total is 10 Ω and the battery current is 2.4 A. The pair has 2.4 × 4.0 = 9.6 V across it, so the 12 Ω resistor dissipates 9.6² ÷ 12 = 7.68 W. 48.0 W puts the full 24 V across it, 69.1 W sends the whole 2.4 A through it, 17.3 W splits the current evenly (1.2 A each), and 12.0 W treats all three resistors as in series (1.0 A).

questions.stem: A battery's terminal voltage is 11.0 V when it supplies 2.0 A and 9.5 V when it supplies 5.0 A. What are its emf and its internal resistance?
questions.explain: V = ε − Ir, so the drop of 1.5 V for 3.0 A more current gives r = 1.5 ÷ 3.0 = 0.500 Ω. Then ε = 11.0 + 2.0 × 0.500 = 12.0 V. 15.0 V and 2.00 Ω invert the ratio (ΔI ÷ ΔV), 11.0 V and 0.500 Ω take the first terminal reading as the emf, 11.0 V and 5.50 Ω give the external load's resistance (11 ÷ 2), and 10.0 V subtracts the Ir drop instead of adding it.

questions.stem: A generating station sends 100 kW to a town at 20,000 V through lines with a total resistance of 8.0 Ω. How much power is lost as heat in the lines?
questions.explain: Line current: I = P ÷ V = 100,000 ÷ 20,000 = 5.0 A. Loss = I²R = 25 × 8.0 = 200 W. 5.0 × 10⁷ W uses V² ÷ R with the full transmission voltage, which is not the voltage across the lines, 40 W is IR, the voltage drop, written as a power, 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ W leaves the power in kilowatts, and 2.0 × 10⁸ W leaves the voltage in kilovolts.

questions.stem: A proton (mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 3.0 × 10⁶ m/s at right angles to a uniform 0.50 T magnetic field. What is the radius of its circular path?
questions.explain: The magnetic force qvB provides the centripetal force mv² ÷ r, so r = mv ÷ qB = (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ × 3.0 × 10⁶) ÷ (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.50) = 5.01 × 10⁻²¹ ÷ 8.0 × 10⁻²⁰ = 0.0626 m. 1.00 × 10⁻²⁰ m leaves out the charge, 16.0 m inverts the fraction, 1.88 × 10⁵ m uses v² on top, and 0.125 m is the diameter of the circle.

questions.stem: A +2.0 μC charge sits at x = 0 and a +8.0 μC charge at x = 0.60 m. How far from the +2.0 μC charge, on the line between them, is the electric field zero?
questions.explain: The fields cancel where kq₁ ÷ x² = kq₂ ÷ (0.60 − x)², so (0.60 − x) ÷ x = √(8.0 ÷ 2.0) = 2 and x = 0.20 m, closer to the smaller charge. 0.40 m measures from the wrong charge, 0.12 m and 0.48 m use the charge ratio without the square root (first one way round, then the other), and 0.30 m is the midpoint, which is only right for equal charges.

questions.stem: A metal rod 0.80 m long slides at a steady 5.0 m/s along two rails in a 0.60 T magnetic field perpendicular to the circuit. The circuit's total resistance is 4.0 Ω. What force must be applied to keep the rod moving at constant speed?
questions.explain: emf = BLv = 0.60 × 0.80 × 5.0 = 2.4 V, so I = 2.4 ÷ 4.0 = 0.60 A.
