The field pushes back on the current with F = BIL = 0.60 × 0.60 × 0.80 = 0.288 N, which the applied force must balance. 0.360 N leaves L out of F = BIL, 1.15 N skips dividing by the resistance, 1.44 N multiplies by v again (that is the power in watts), and 0.480 N leaves B out of F = BIL.

questions.stem: A water heater on 240 V draws 12.5 A and is 90% efficient. How long does it take to heat 150 kg of water from 15 °C to 60 °C? (c = 4,186 J/kg·°C)
questions.explain: Heat needed: 150 × 4,186 × 45 = 2.83 × 10⁷ J. Electrical power = 240 × 12.5 = 3,000 W, of which 90% (2,700 W) heats the water. t = 2.83 × 10⁷ ÷ 2,700 = 10,470 s = 2.91 h. 2.62 h ignores the efficiency, 2.35 h applies the efficiency the wrong way (3,000 ÷ 0.90), 3.88 h uses the final 60 °C as the temperature rise, and 0.969 h uses the starting 15 °C as the rise.

questions.stem: An ambulance siren sounds at 700 Hz. The ambulance drives straight toward a stationary listener at 30 m/s, and sound travels at 340 m/s. What frequency does the listener hear?
questions.explain: For a moving source, f′ = f × v ÷ (v − v_s) = 700 × 340 ÷ 310 = 768 Hz. 643 Hz uses the receding formula (v + v_s), 762 Hz uses the moving-listener formula (v + v_o) ÷ v, which does not apply when the source moves, 730 Hz simply adds 30 Hz, and 700 Hz ignores the Doppler shift.

questions.stem: An object stands 30 cm in front of a converging lens of focal length 20 cm. Where is the image, and how does it compare with the object?
questions.explain: 1/d_i = 1/f − 1/d_o = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60, so d_i = 60 cm on the far side, a real image. Magnification = −d_i ÷ d_o = −2.0: inverted and twice as tall. 12 cm adds the reciprocals, 10 cm simply subtracts 30 − 20, 0.50 times inverts the magnification ratio (d_o ÷ d_i), and 50 cm adds 30 + 20.

questions.stem: Light travels in glass (n = 1.50) toward a boundary with water (n = 1.33). To the nearest tenth of a degree, what is the critical angle for total internal reflection?
questions.explain: sin c = n₂ ÷ n₁ = 1.33 ÷ 1.50 = 0.887, so c = 62.5°. Because water bends light less than air does, the critical angle is larger than the glass-to-air value. 41.8° is the glass-to-air angle (1 ÷ 1.50), 27.5° is the complement measured from the surface, 48.8° is the water-to-air angle (1 ÷ 1.33), and 9.8° subtracts the indices (sin c = 0.17).

questions.stem: An air bubble of volume 2.00 cm³ is released 30 m below the surface of the sea, where the water is 7 °C, and rises to the surface, where the water is 27 °C. Seawater density is 1,025 kg/m³, atmospheric pressure is 101 kPa and g = 9.8 m/s². What is its volume at the surface?
questions.explain: Absolute pressure at depth = 101 + 1,025 × 9.8 × 30 ÷ 1,000 = 402 kPa. V₂ = V₁ × (P₁ ÷ P₂) × (T₂ ÷ T₁) = 2.00 × (402 ÷ 101) × (300 ÷ 280) = 8.54 cm³. 7.97 cm³ ignores the temperature change, 30.7 cm³ uses Celsius temperatures (27 ÷ 7), 6.39 cm³ uses gauge pressure at depth and forgets the atmosphere, and 0.469 cm³ inverts both ratios.

questions.stem: How much heat is needed to turn 0.20 kg of water at 40 °C completely into steam at 100 °C? (c = 4,186 J/kg·°C, latent heat of vaporization = 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg)
questions.explain: Warm to 100 °C: 0.20 × 4,186 × 60 = 50.2 kJ. Boil: 0.20 × 2.26 × 10⁶ = 452 kJ. Total = 502 kJ. 452 kJ leaves out the warming, 50.2 kJ leaves out the boiling, 536 kJ warms through 100 °C instead of 60 °C, and 2,310 kJ forgets to multiply the latent heat by the 0.20 kg mass.

questions.stem: Water flows horizontally at 2.0 m/s and 150 kPa through a pipe of cross-section 10 cm², which narrows to 2.5 cm². What is the pressure in the narrow section? (water density 1,000 kg/m³)
questions.explain: Continuity: the area falls by a factor of 4, so the speed rises to 8.0 m/s. Bernoulli: ΔP = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = ½ × 1,000 × (64 − 4) = 30 kPa, and the pressure falls where the water speeds up: 150 − 30 = 120 kPa. 180 kPa adds the change, 147 kPa forgets to square the speeds, 90 kPa drops the ½, and 118 kPa uses ½ρv₂² alone and ignores the 2.0 m/s already in the wide pipe.

questions.stem: A pipe 0.85 m long is closed at one end and open at the other. Sound travels at 340 m/s. What are its two lowest resonant frequencies?
questions.explain: A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so the fundamental has λ = 4L = 3.4 m and f = 340 ÷ 3.4 = 100 Hz. Only odd harmonics occur, so the next is 300 Hz. 200 and 400 Hz are the open-pipe values, 100 and 200 Hz include an even harmonic a closed pipe cannot have, 400 and 1,200 Hz take λ = L, and 200 and 600 Hz take λ = 2L.

questions.stem: A copper rod 0.50 m long with a cross-section of 2.0 cm² has one end at 100 °C and the other at 20 °C. Copper's thermal conductivity is 400 W/(m·K). How much heat flows along the rod each minute?
questions.explain: Rate: P = kAΔT ÷ L = 400 × 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 80 ÷ 0.50 = 12.8 W. In 60 s: 12.8 × 60 = 768 J. 12.8 J is the heat per second, 7.68 × 10⁶ J leaves the area in cm², 192 J multiplies by the length instead of dividing, and 1,152 J adds the end temperatures (120) instead of subtracting them.

questions.stem: The sound level 4.0 m from a pump is 90 dB. Treating the pump as a point source radiating evenly, what is the sound level 40 m from it?
questions.explain: Intensity follows the inverse square law, so 10 times the distance gives 1/100 of the intensity. A factor of 100 in intensity is 10 log 100 = 20 dB, so the level is 90 − 20 = 70 dB. 80 dB lets intensity fall only as 1/r, 9.0 dB and 0.90 dB divide the decibel number itself by 10 and by 100, and 45 dB halves the decibel value.

questions.stem: An ion of iron-56 (atomic number 26) has 23 electrons. What are its charge and its number of neutrons?
questions.explain: Atomic number 26 means 26 protons. Charge = protons − electrons = 26 − 23 = +3, and neutrons = mass number − protons = 56 − 26 = 30. Fe³⁻ gets the sign backwards (losing electrons makes a positive ion), 26 neutrons assumes neutrons equal protons, 33 neutrons subtracts the electrons from 56, and Fe²⁺ assumes iron's other common ion instead of counting.

questions.stem: Copper has two natural isotopes: copper-63 (62.93 u, 69.15% abundance) and copper-65 (64.93 u, 30.85%). What is copper's average atomic mass?
questions.explain: Weight each isotope's mass by its fraction: 62.93 × 0.6915 + 64.93 × 0.3085 = 43.516 + 20.031 = 63.55 u. 63.93 u is the plain average of the two masses, 64.31 u swaps the abundances, 63.62 u uses the mass numbers 63 and 65 instead of the isotope masses, and 62.93 u is just the more abundant isotope.

questions.stem: Boron's average atomic mass is 10.81 u. Its isotopes are boron-10 (10.013 u) and boron-11 (11.009 u). What is the percent abundance of boron-11?
questions.explain: Let x be the fraction of boron-11: 10.013(1 − x) + 11.009x = 10.81, so 0.996x = 0.797 and x = 0.800, or 80.0%. 20.0% is the abundance of boron-10, 79.7% stops at 0.797 without dividing by 0.996, 50.0% assumes equal amounts, and 81.0% reads the decimal part of 10.81 as a percent.

questions.stem: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of chromium (Z = 24)?
questions.explain: Chromium is a known exception: moving one 4s electron into 3d gives a half-filled 3d subshell, which is more stable, so the configuration is [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ (18 + 1 + 5 = 24 electrons). [Ar] 4s² 3d⁴ is what plain filling order predicts, [Ar] 4s² 3d⁵ has 25 electrons (manganese), [Ar] 3d⁶ empties 4s entirely, and [Ar] 4s² 4p⁴ skips the 3d subshell.

questions.stem: How many unpaired electrons does the Fe³⁺ ion have in its ground state? (Fe, Z = 26)
questions.explain: Iron is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. Ions of transition metals lose their 4s electrons first, so Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵, and by Hund's rule each of the five d orbitals holds one electron: 5 unpaired. 4 is the count for neutral iron (3d⁶), 3 removes all three electrons from 3d (4s² 3d³), 1 pairs electrons before every orbital has one, and 6 counts every 3d electron of the neutral atom as unpaired.

questions.stem: Which lists Na, Mg, Al, P and S in order of increasing first ionization energy?
questions.explain: Ionization energy rises across period 3, with two dips. Al is below Mg because its outermost electron is a lone 3p electron, easier to remove than one from Mg's filled 3s. S is below P because S has its first paired 3p electron, and the repulsion makes it easier to remove. Na < Mg < Al < P < S ignores both dips, the next two options include only one dip each, and the last option reverses the trend.

questions.stem: Which of these species has the largest radius: S²⁻, Cl⁻, Ar, K⁺ or Ca²⁺?
questions.explain: All five have 18 electrons, so the size depends on how many protons pull on that same electron cloud. S²⁻ has the fewest protons (16), so its electrons are held least tightly and it is the largest. Ca²⁺ (20 protons) is the smallest, which makes it the trap for anyone who picks the heaviest atom. Ar sits in the middle, and K⁺ and Cl⁻ are smaller and larger than Ar respectively, but neither beats S²⁻.

questions.stem: Electronegativities: H 2.1, C 2.5, N 3.0, O 3.5, F 4.0. Which bond is the most polar?
questions.explain: Polarity grows with the electronegativity difference: C-F is 4.0 − 2.5 = 1.5, O-H is 3.5 − 2.1 = 1.4, C-O is 1.0, N-H is 0.9 and N-F is 1.0. O-H is the usual pick because water is so polar, but 1.4 is just short of 1.5. The two 1.0 bonds are moderately polar, and N-H is the least polar here.

questions.stem: What is the molecular shape of ammonia, NH₃, and is the molecule polar?
questions.explain: Nitrogen has three bonding pairs and one lone pair. The four electron groups point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, but the shape is named from the atoms only, so NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal. The lone pair makes the molecule lopsided, so the bond dipoles don't cancel and it is polar. Trigonal planar ignores the lone pair, tetrahedral names the electron-group geometry instead of the shape, and nonpolar assumes the dipoles cancel.

questions.stem: Which molecule is nonpolar even though every one of its bonds is polar?
questions.explain: CO₂ is linear (no lone pairs on carbon), so its two equal C=O dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel. H₂O and SO₂ look similar on paper but are bent because of lone pairs on the central atom, so their dipoles add. NH₃ is pyramidal, and in CH₂Cl₂ the C-Cl and C-H bonds differ, so the dipoles can't cancel.

questions.stem: Which compound contains both ionic and covalent bonds?
questions.explain: K₂SO₄ is made of K⁺ ions held ionically to sulfate ions, and inside each sulfate ion the S and O atoms share electrons covalently. KCl and MgO are ionic only, because each is a simple metal ion paired with a nonmetal ion. CH₃OH and SO₃ are covalent only, because they contain no metal ion at all.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons must be shown in the Lewis structure of the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻?
questions.explain: Sulfur and oxygen are both in group 16, so each brings 6 valence electrons: 6 + 4 × 6 = 30. The 2− charge means two extra electrons, so the total is 32. 30 forgets the charge, 28 subtracts the charge as if it were positive, 34 adds 4 (one per oxygen), and 24 counts only the oxygens.

questions.stem: Aluminum forms Al³⁺ and sulfate is SO₄²⁻. What is the formula of aluminum sulfate, and how many oxygen atoms are in one formula unit?
questions.explain: Balance the charges: 2 × (+3) = +6 and 3 × (−2) = −6, so the formula is Al₂(SO₄)₃. The subscript 3 multiplies everything in the bracket, so there are 3 × 4 = 12 oxygen atoms. Al₃(SO₄)₂ swaps the subscripts, 4 oxygens ignores the 3 outside the bracket, 7 adds 4 + 3 instead of multiplying, and AlSO₄ doesn't balance the charges.

questions.stem: Atom X has a mass number of 81 and 46 neutrons. Which element is X, and how many electrons does the ion X⁻ have?
questions.explain: Protons = 81 − 46 = 35, and atomic number 35 is bromine. A 1− charge means one extra electron: 35 + 1 = 36. 34 subtracts the extra electron, 35 ignores the charge, palladium (Z = 46) uses the neutron count as the atomic number, and thallium (Z = 81) uses the mass number as the atomic number.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy the n = 4 shell?
questions.explain: A shell holds 2n² electrons: 2 × 4² = 32 (4s 2, 4p 6, 4d 10, 4f 14). 18 is the n = 3 shell, 16 is n² × 1 instead of 2n², 8 is the octet rule, which describes valence shells in bonding and not shell capacity, and 14 is the 4f subshell alone.

questions.stem: How many water molecules are in 9.0 g of water? (H 1.0, O 16.0, Avogadro's number 6.02 × 10²³)
questions.explain: Water's molar mass is 18.0 g/mol, so 9.0 g is 0.50 mol, and 0.50 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules. 5.42 × 10²⁴ multiplies the grams by Avogadro's number, 3.34 × 10²² divides Avogadro's number by 18 and drops the 9.0 g, 6.02 × 10²³ assumes one mole, and 9.03 × 10²³ counts atoms (3 per molecule) instead of molecules.

questions.stem: What is the percent by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃? (N 14.0, H 1.0, O 16.0)
questions.explain: There are two nitrogens, one in NH₄⁺ and one in NO₃⁻. Molar mass = 2(14.0) + 4(1.0) + 3(16.0) = 80.0 g/mol, so %N = 28.0 ÷ 80.0 = 35.0%. 17.5% counts only one nitrogen, 22.2% is the fraction of atoms (2 of 9) rather than mass, 60.0% is the oxygen percentage, and 5.0% is the hydrogen percentage.

questions.stem: A compound is 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass, and its molar mass is 180 g/mol. What is its molecular formula? (C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0)
questions.explain: In 100 g: 40.0 ÷ 12.0 = 3.33 mol C, 6.7 ÷ 1.0 = 6.7 mol H and 53.3 ÷ 16.0 = 3.33 mol O, a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio, so the empirical formula is CH₂O (30 g/mol). 180 ÷ 30 = 6, giving C₆H₁₂O₆. CH₂O stops at the empirical formula, C₃H₆O₃ (90 g/mol) and C₂H₄O₂ (60 g/mol) use the wrong multiple, and C₄H₇O₄ reads the percentages as rough atom counts.

questions.stem: A 2.50 g sample of an iron oxide contains 1.75 g of iron. What is its empirical formula? (Fe 55.8, O 16.0)
questions.explain: Oxygen = 2.50 − 1.75 = 0.75 g. Moles: Fe 1.75 ÷ 55.8 = 0.0314 and O 0.75 ÷ 16.0 = 0.0469. O : Fe = 1.49, about 1.5, so doubling gives Fe₂O₃. FeO rounds 1.5 down to 1, Fe₃O₄ uses a 1.33 ratio, FeO₂ rounds 1.5 up to 2, and Fe₃O₂ inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: When C₄H₁₀ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O is balanced with the smallest whole-number coefficients, what is the coefficient of O₂?
questions.explain: For one butane: 4 CO₂ and 5 H₂O, which hold 8 + 5 = 13 oxygen atoms, so 6.5 O₂. Whole numbers require doubling everything: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O. 6.5 is right for one butane but isn't a whole number, 26 counts oxygen atoms instead of O₂ molecules, 9 adds the product coefficients for one butane, and 18 adds the doubled product coefficients.

questions.stem: For 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃, what mass of AlCl₃ forms from 5.40 g of aluminum with excess chlorine? (Al 27.0, Cl 35.5)
questions.explain: 5.40 ÷ 27.0 = 0.200 mol Al. The ratio Al : AlCl₃ is 2 : 2, so 0.200 mol AlCl₃ × 133.5 g/mol = 26.7 g. 40.1 g uses the 3 : 2 ratio of Cl₂ instead, 21.3 g is the mass of Cl₂ consumed (0.300 mol × 71.0), 17.8 g uses a 2 : 3 ratio, and 13.4 g uses a 2 : 1 ratio.

questions.stem: For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, 28.0 g of N₂ reacts with 4.5 g of H₂. What is the maximum mass of NH₃ that can form? (N 14.0, H 1.0)
questions.explain: N₂: 28.0 ÷ 28.0 = 1.00 mol. H₂: 4.5 ÷ 2.0 = 2.25 mol, which would need only 0.75 mol N₂, so H₂ is limiting. NH₃ = 2.25 × 2/3 = 1.50 mol × 17.0 = 25.5 g. 34.0 g assumes N₂ is limiting, 32.5 g adds the reactant masses (impossible when one is left over), 76.5 g forgets the 3 : 2 ratio and doubles, and 38.3 g uses a 1 : 1 ratio.

questions.stem: Heating 50.0 g of CaCO₃ (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂) produces 22.4 g of CaO. What is the percent yield? (Ca 40.0, C 12.0, O 16.0)
questions.explain: CaCO₃ is 100 g/mol, so 50.0 g is 0.500 mol, which gives at most 0.500 mol CaO × 56.0 = 28.0 g. Percent yield = 22.4 ÷ 28.0 = 80.0%. 44.8% divides by the starting mass instead of the theoretical yield, 125% divides the wrong way, 56.0% is the theoretical yield over the starting mass, and 20.0% is the shortfall, not the yield.

questions.stem: For 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂, what volume of O₂ at STP comes from 6.80 g of H₂O₂? (H 1.0, O 16.0, 22.4 L/mol at STP)
questions.explain: H₂O₂ is 34.0 g/mol, so 6.80 g is 0.200 mol. Two H₂O₂ give one O₂, so 0.100 mol O₂ × 22.4 L/mol = 2.24 L. 4.48 L ignores the 2 : 1 ratio, 1.12 L halves twice, 152 L multiplies the grams by 22.4, and 0.100 L reports the moles as liters.

questions.stem: How many oxygen atoms are in 0.250 mol of calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂? (Avogadro's number 6.02 × 10²³)
questions.explain: Each Ca(NO₃)₂ has 2 × 3 = 6 oxygen atoms, so 0.250 × 6 = 1.50 mol O, and 1.50 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²³. 4.52 × 10²³ counts 3 O and ignores the subscript 2, 1.51 × 10²³ counts formula units, 3.61 × 10²⁴ drops the 0.250 mol, and 3.01 × 10²³ counts only the 2 outside the bracket.

questions.stem: What percent of the mass of copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate, CuSO₄·5H₂O, is water? (Cu 63.5, S 32.1, O 16.0, H 1.0)
questions.explain: CuSO₄ = 63.5 + 32.1 + 64.0 = 159.6 g/mol and 5H₂O = 90.0 g/mol, so the hydrate is 249.6 g/mol and water is 90.0 ÷ 249.6 = 36.1%. 56.4% divides by the anhydrous mass only, 63.9% is the CuSO₄ share, 10.1% uses a single water over CuSO₄·H₂O, and 7.2% puts one water's mass over the full hydrate.

questions.stem: Complete combustion of 0.10 mol of a hydrocarbon produces 0.40 mol of CO₂ and 0.50 mol of H₂O. What is the hydrocarbon's formula?
questions.explain: Per mole of fuel: 0.40 ÷ 0.10 = 4 C, and each H₂O carries 2 H, so 0.50 × 2 ÷ 0.10 = 10 H: C₄H₁₀. C₄H₅ counts one H per water, C₂H₅ is the empirical formula, C₄H₈ assumes the CₙH₂ₙ pattern without calculating, and C₄H₁₀O puts oxygen in the fuel, but the oxygen in the products comes from the O₂.

questions.stem: For 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, 6.9 g of sodium reacts with 7.1 g of chlorine gas. Which reactant is in excess, and what mass of it is left over? (Na 23.0, Cl 35.5)
questions.explain: Na: 6.9 ÷ 23.0 = 0.30 mol. Cl₂: 7.1 ÷ 71.0 = 0.10 mol, which uses 0.20 mol Na. Left over: 0.10 mol Na × 23.0 = 2.3 g. 4.6 g uses a 1 : 1 ratio, 5.75 g turns the 2 : 1 ratio upside down, 3.35 g applies the 2 : 1 ratio to grams instead of moles, and 0.10 g reports the leftover moles as grams.

questions.stem: What is the mass of a single gold atom? (Au 197, Avogadro's number 6.02 × 10²³)
questions.explain: One mole (6.02 × 10²³ atoms) has a mass of 197 g, so one atom is 197 ÷ 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.27 × 10⁻²² g. 1.19 × 10²⁶ multiplies instead of dividing, 3.06 × 10²¹ divides the wrong way round, 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g is the mass of 1 u and forgets the 197, and 3.27 × 10⁻²⁵ g divides by an extra 1,000 as if converting to kilograms.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 2.00 L at 27 °C and 1.00 atm. What volume does it occupy at 127 °C and 2.00 atm?
questions.explain: Convert to kelvin: 300 K and 400 K. V₂ = V₁ × (P₁/P₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 2.00 × (1.00/2.00) × (400/300) = 1.33 L. 4.70 L uses Celsius temperatures (127/27), 5.33 L multiplies by the pressure ratio the wrong way, 0.750 L inverts the temperature ratio, and 1.00 L ignores the temperature change.

questions.stem: How many moles of gas are in a 4.10 L container at 2.00 atm and 27 °C? (R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K))
questions.explain: n = PV ÷ RT = (2.00 × 4.10) ÷ (0.0821 × 300) = 8.20 ÷ 24.6 = 0.333 mol. 3.70 mol uses 27 instead of 300 K, 0.166 mol leaves out the pressure, 3.00 mol computes RT ÷ PV, and 0.366 mol uses 273 K (STP temperature) instead of the actual 300 K.

questions.stem: A container holds 8.0 g of He, 16.0 g of O₂ and 14.0 g of N₂ at a total pressure of 1.20 atm. What is the partial pressure of O₂? (He 4.0, O 16.0, N 14.0)
questions.explain: Moles: He 2.0, O₂ 0.50, N₂ 0.50, total 3.0. The mole fraction of O₂ is 0.50 ÷ 3.0 = 1/6, so P = 1.20 ÷ 6 = 0.20 atm. 0.51 atm uses the mass fraction (16/38), 0.40 atm splits the pressure equally three ways, 0.60 atm ignores the helium, and 0.30 atm treats helium as He₂ (1.0 mol instead of 2.0).

questions.stem: A balloon holds 3.00 L of gas at −23 °C. At constant pressure, what is its volume at 77 °C?
questions.explain: Kelvin temperatures: −23 + 273 = 250 K and 77 + 273 = 350 K. V₂ = 3.00 × 350/250 = 4.20 L. 2.14 L inverts the ratio, 10.0 L uses Celsius values and drops the minus sign (77/23), 3.85 L uses 273 K as the starting temperature, and 3.00 L assumes warming changes only the pressure.

questions.stem: What mass of NaOH is needed to make 250. mL of 0.400 M solution? (Na 23.0, O 16.0, H 1.0)
questions.explain: Moles = M × V = 0.400 × 0.250 L = 0.100 mol, and 0.100 × 40.0 g/mol = 4.00 g. 16.0 g is the mass for a full liter, 4,000 g uses 250 L instead of 0.250 L, 25.0 g divides the volume by the molarity, and 0.100 g reports the moles as grams.

questions.stem: What volume of 12.0 M HCl is needed to prepare 3.00 L of 0.500 M HCl?
questions.explain: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂, so V₁ = (0.500 × 3.00) ÷ 12.0 = 0.125 L = 125 mL. 72.0 L inverts the concentrations, 2.88 L is the water you'd add rather than the acid you need, 12.5 mL and 1.25 L are decimal-point slips in the liter to milliliter conversion.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.0050 M H₂SO₄, assuming both protons ionize completely?
questions.explain: Two protons per H₂SO₄ make [H⁺] = 2 × 0.0050 = 0.010 M, and pH = −log(0.010) = 2.00. 2.30 counts only one proton, 12.00 is 14 − 2.00 (a pOH mix-up), 1.70 counts four protons (0.020 M), and 2.60 halves the concentration instead of doubling it.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.020 M Ba(OH)₂, a strong base?
questions.explain: Each Ba(OH)₂ releases two OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 0.040 M, pOH = −log(0.040) = 1.40 and pH = 14.00 − 1.40 = 12.60. 12.30 counts one OH⁻, 1.40 stops at the pOH, 1.70 is the pOH with one OH⁻, and 12.90 doubles twice (0.080 M).

questions.stem: 25.0 mL of H₂SO₄ is exactly neutralized by 30.0 mL of 0.200 M NaOH. What is the molarity of the acid?
questions.explain: NaOH: 0.200 × 0.0300 = 0.00600 mol. H₂SO₄ gives two H⁺, so it needs half as many moles: 0.00300 mol ÷ 0.0250 L = 0.120 M. 0.240 M uses a 1 : 1 ratio, 0.167 M swaps the two volumes, 0.0833 M swaps the volumes and halves, and 0.0545 M divides by the combined 55.0 mL.

questions.stem: Acetic acid has Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. What is the pH of a 0.10 M acetic acid solution?
questions.explain: For a weak acid, [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka × C) = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.34 × 10⁻³ M, so pH = 2.87. 1.00 treats acetic acid as a strong acid, 4.74 is the pKa, 5.74 is −log(Ka × C) without the square root, and 2.37 halves the pKa and forgets the concentration.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg water sample contains 3.0 mg of lead. What is the lead concentration in parts per million?
questions.explain: 1 ppm is 1 mg per kg of water, so 3.0 mg ÷ 2.0 kg = 1.5 ppm. 1,500 ppm treats the 2.0 kg as 2.0 g, 0.0015 ppm treats the 3.0 mg as 3.0 µg, 6.0 ppm multiplies instead of dividing, and 0.67 ppm divides the wrong way round.

questions.stem: 100. mL of 0.30 M NaCl is mixed with 200. mL of 0.60 M NaCl. What is the NaCl concentration of the mixture?
questions.explain: Total moles = 0.100 × 0.30 + 0.200 × 0.60 = 0.030 + 0.120 = 0.150 mol, in 0.300 L, so 0.50 M. 0.45 M is the plain average, 0.90 M adds the concentrations, 0.40 M swaps the volumes, and 0.15 M reports the moles instead of the molarity.

questions.stem: What is the density of carbon dioxide gas at STP? (C 12.0, O 16.0, 22.4 L/mol at STP)
questions.explain: One mole of CO₂ (44.0 g) fills 22.4 L at STP, so density = 44.0 ÷ 22.4 = 1.96 g/L. 0.509 g/L divides the wrong way, 1.25 g/L uses CO (28.0 g/mol), 44.0 g/L forgets to divide by the molar volume, and 1.43 g/L uses O₂ (32.0 g/mol).

questions.stem: What is the conjugate base of the hydrogen phosphate ion, HPO₄²⁻?
questions.explain: A conjugate base is the acid minus one H⁺: remove the hydrogen and the charge drops by one, giving PO₄³⁻. H₂PO₄⁻ is the conjugate acid (one H⁺ added), H₃PO₄ adds two, PO₄²⁻ removes the hydrogen but forgets to change the charge, and HPO₄³⁻ changes the charge without removing the hydrogen.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of chromium in potassium dichromate, K₂Cr₂O₇?
questions.explain: The oxidation numbers must sum to zero: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0, so 2x = 12 and x = +6. +12 forgets to divide between the two chromium atoms, +7 leaves out the potassium, +3 is chromium's common ion charge rather than its value here, and −6 gets the sign backwards.

questions.stem: In the reaction Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s), which species is the oxidizing agent?
questions.explain: Cu²⁺ gains two electrons and becomes Cu, so it is reduced, and the species that is reduced is the oxidizing agent. Zn loses electrons and is the reducing agent, the classic swap. Sulfate is a spectator ion that doesn't change, and Cu and Zn²⁺ are products, not agents.

questions.stem: When MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ is balanced in acid, how many Fe²⁺ ions react with each MnO₄⁻ ion?
questions.explain: Manganese goes from +7 in MnO₄⁻ to +2, gaining 5 electrons. Each Fe²⁺ loses 1 electron becoming Fe³⁺, so 5 Fe²⁺ are needed: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O. 1 assumes a 1 : 1 ratio, 2 uses the charge of Mn²⁺, 7 uses manganese's starting oxidation number, and 8 is the coefficient of H⁺.

questions.stem: Which single-replacement reaction actually takes place as written?
questions.explain: A metal replaces hydrogen or another metal only if it is more active. Magnesium is above hydrogen in the activity series, so it reacts with acid. Copper, silver and gold are below hydrogen, and silver is below zinc, so those reactions don't happen. AgNO₃ + NaCl does happen, but it is a double-replacement (precipitation) reaction, not a single replacement.

questions.stem: What is the net ionic equation when solutions of BaCl₂ and Na₂SO₄ are mixed?
questions.explain: Barium sulfate is insoluble, so it precipitates, and the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions stay dissolved as spectators. The net ionic equation keeps only the ions that change: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s). NaCl is soluble, so it doesn't precipitate, the full molecular equation isn't a net ionic equation, and BaCl₂ and Na₂SO₄ are the soluble starting salts.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in the thiosulfate ion, S₂O₃²⁻?
questions.explain: The oxidation numbers must add up to the ion's charge: 2x + 3(−2) = −2, so 2x = +4 and x = +2. +4 forgets to divide between the two sulfur atoms, +6 is sulfur's value in sulfate, +3 ignores the 2− charge (2x = 6), and −2 is sulfur's value in sulfide.

questions.stem: Uranium-238 (Z = 92) undergoes alpha decay. What is the product nucleus?
questions.explain: An alpha particle is ⁴He: 2 protons and 2 neutrons. Mass number 238 − 4 = 234, atomic number 92 − 2 = 90, which is thorium. Plutonium adds the 2 protons instead of subtracting them, ²³⁸Np describes beta-minus decay, ²³⁶Th removes only 2 from the mass number, and ²³⁴U forgets to change the element.

questions.stem: Uranium-238 (Z = 92) decays through a series of steps to lead-206 (Z = 82). How many alpha and beta-minus decays occur in total?
questions.explain: Only alpha decay changes the mass number: (238 − 206) ÷ 4 = 8 alphas, which would lower Z by 16 to 76. Lead is 82, so 6 beta-minus decays (each raises Z by 1) bring it back up. 10 beta-minus decays uses the plain Z difference, 6 and 8 swaps the counts, positrons would lower Z further, and 16 alphas divides the mass change by 2 instead of 4.

questions.stem: Carbon-11 (Z = 6) decays by positron emission. What is the product nucleus?
questions.explain: In positron emission a proton becomes a neutron, so Z falls by 1 and the mass number stays the same: ¹¹C → ¹¹B + e⁺. ¹¹N raises Z, which is beta-minus decay, ⁷Be is alpha decay, ¹⁰B removes a nucleon that isn't lost, and ¹¹Be drops Z by 2 as if a positron carried double charge.

questions.stem: In the fission reaction ²³⁵U + ¹n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + x ¹n, what is x? (U Z = 92, Ba Z = 56, Kr Z = 36)
questions.explain: Mass numbers must balance: 235 + 1 = 236 on the left, and 141 + 92 = 233 on the right, so 3 neutrons. The atomic numbers already balance (92 = 56 + 36). 2 forgets the incoming neutron, 1 counts only the neutron that started the reaction, 4 counts the incoming neutron twice, and 0 assumes the fragments account for every nucleon.

questions.stem: Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8.0 days. How much of a 200. mg sample remains after 32 days?
questions.explain: 32 ÷ 8.0 = 4 half-lives: 200 → 100 → 50 → 25 → 12.5 mg. 25.0 mg stops after three halvings, 50.0 mg divides by the number of half-lives (200 ÷ 4) instead of halving four times, 6.25 mg halves five times, and 187.5 mg is the amount that has decayed, not what remains.

questions.stem: A sample's activity falls from 960 counts per minute to 60 counts per minute in 12 hours. What is its half-life?
questions.explain: 960 ÷ 60 = 16 = 2⁴, so 4 half-lives passed: 12 ÷ 4 = 3.0 hours. 0.75 hours divides by 16 instead of by the number of halvings, 4.0 hours counts three halvings, 2.4 hours counts the five values 960, 480, 240, 120, 60 as five half-lives, and 1.5 hours divides by 8.

questions.stem: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years. A bone has lost 87.5% of its original carbon-14. How old is it?
questions.explain: If 87.5% is gone, 12.5% = 1/8 remains, which is 3 half-lives: 3 × 5,730 = 17,190 years. 11,460 years is 2 half-lives (25% left), 22,920 years is 4, 5,014 years multiplies 0.875 by one half-life, and 40,110 years reads 7/8 as 7 half-lives.

questions.stem: Cobalt-60 has a half-life of 5.27 years. What percent of a sample remains after 10.0 years?
questions.explain: The fraction left is (1/2)^(t ÷ T½) = (1/2)^(10.0 ÷ 5.27) = (1/2)^1.90 = 0.268, or 26.8%. 5.1% assumes a straight-line loss of 50% per half-life, 69.4% inverts the exponent (5.27 ÷ 10.0), 52.7% is just 5.27 ÷ 10.0, and 25.0% rounds to exactly two half-lives.

questions.stem: Which radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper or the outer layer of skin but is the most damaging if a source that emits it is inhaled or swallowed?
questions.explain: Alpha particles are heavy and doubly charged, so they lose energy fast: paper or dead skin stops them outside the body. Inside the body, they deposit all that energy in a tiny volume of living tissue, which makes them the most damaging internal hazard. Beta particles need a few millimeters of aluminum or plastic, gamma rays need dense shielding such as lead or concrete, neutrons pass through paper easily, and positrons behave like beta particles.

questions.stem: The half-value layer of lead for a certain gamma ray is 1.0 cm. What thickness of lead reduces the gamma intensity to 1/32 of its unshielded value?
questions.explain: Each half-value layer halves the intensity, and 1/32 = (1/2)⁵, so 5 layers × 1.0 cm = 5.0 cm. 32 cm treats the reduction as linear, 16 cm halves 32, 6.0 cm counts 2⁶ = 64, and 3.2 cm is a decimal slip on 32.

questions.stem: Which material is the most effective at slowing down fast neutrons?
questions.explain: A neutron loses the most energy in a collision with a nucleus of about its own mass. Hydrogen nuclei are single protons, almost the same mass as a neutron, so hydrogen-rich materials like water slow neutrons best. Lead, steel and tungsten are excellent gamma shields because they are dense, but their heavy nuclei let neutrons bounce off with little energy loss. Thin aluminum foil stops only alpha and some beta particles.

questions.stem: A helium-4 nucleus has a mass of 4.00150 u (the neutral atom is 4.00260 u). A proton is 1.00728 u and a neutron is 1.00866 u. What is the nuclear binding energy? (1 u = 931.5 MeV)
questions.explain: Separate nucleons: 2(1.00728) + 2(1.00866) = 4.03188 u. Mass defect = 4.03188 − 4.00150 = 0.03038 u, and 0.03038 × 931.5 = 28.3 MeV. 7.07 MeV is the binding energy per nucleon, 3,727 MeV converts the whole nucleus mass, 0.0304 MeV forgets the 931.5 conversion, and 27.3 MeV uses the neutral atom's mass, which includes two electrons the proton masses leave out.

questions.stem: If 1.0 g of mass is converted completely into energy, how much energy is released? (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s)
questions.explain: E = mc² with mass in kilograms: 0.0010 kg × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 0.0010 × 9.00 × 10¹⁶ = 9.0 × 10¹³ J. 9.0 × 10¹⁶ J leaves the mass in grams, 3.0 × 10⁵ J forgets to square c, 9.0 × 10¹⁰ J converts grams to kilograms twice, and 4.5 × 10¹³ J uses ½mc² as if it were kinetic energy.

questions.stem: Why do both the fission of uranium and the fusion of hydrogen release energy?
options: Both form products with more binding energy per nucleon, closer to iron-56.
Both form products with more total mass than the starting nuclei.
Both break nuclear bonds, and breaking any bond releases energy.
Both convert neutrons into protons, which have less mass.
Fission lowers and fusion raises the binding energy per nucleon.
questions.explain: Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56. Splitting a heavy nucleus or joining light ones both move toward that peak, so the products are more tightly bound, slightly lighter, and the lost mass is released as energy (E = mc²). The products have less mass, not more. Breaking bonds always absorbs energy, a proton is lighter than a neutron but that isn't why fission and fusion release energy, and both processes raise the binding energy per nucleon.

questions.stem: A radioactive source has an activity of 2.0 mCi. What is its activity in becquerels? (1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq)
questions.explain: 2.0 mCi = 2.0 × 10⁻³ Ci, and 2.0 × 10⁻³ × 3.7 × 10¹⁰ = 7.4 × 10⁷ Bq (decays per second). 7.4 × 10¹⁰ forgets the milli prefix, 7.4 × 10¹³ treats milli as × 1,000, 1.85 × 10⁷ divides by 2 instead of multiplying, and 7.4 × 10⁴ treats mCi as microcuries.

questions.stem: How much heat is needed to warm 250 g of water from 20.0 °C to 80.0 °C? (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C))
questions.explain: q = mcΔT = 250 × 4.18 × 60.0 = 62,700 J = 62.7 kJ. 83.6 kJ uses the final temperature (80.0) as ΔT, 20.9 kJ uses the starting temperature, 15.0 kJ leaves out the specific heat, and 6.27 kJ reads 4.18 as 0.418.

questions.stem: 100. g of water at 80.0 °C is mixed with 300. g of water at 20.0 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?
questions.explain: Heat lost by the hot water equals heat gained by the cold: 100(80.0 − T) = 300(T − 20.0), so 8,000 + 6,000 = 400T and T = 35.0 °C. 50.0 °C is the plain average, 65.0 °C swaps the masses, 60.0 °C is the temperature difference, and 15.0 °C is the rise of the cold water without adding its starting 20.0 °C.

questions.stem: A 50.0 g metal block at 100.0 °C is dropped into 100.0 g of water at 20.0 °C. The final temperature is 25.0 °C. What is the specific heat of the metal? (water c = 4.18 J/(g·°C))
questions.explain: Heat gained by water = 100.0 × 4.18 × 5.0 = 2,090 J. The metal lost the same heat while cooling 75.0 °C, so c = 2,090 ÷ (50.0 × 75.0) = 0.557 J/(g·°C). 0.523 uses 80.0 °C (the gap between the starting temperatures) for the metal, 0.279 swaps the two masses, 0.133 leaves out water's specific heat, and 1.67 uses the final temperature (25.0) as the metal's ΔT.

questions.stem: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ. CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −283.0 kJ. What is ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g)?
questions.explain: Keep the first equation and reverse the second (CO₂ → CO + ½O₂, ΔH = +283.0 kJ). Adding them cancels the CO₂ and leaves C + ½O₂ → CO, so ΔH = −393.5 + 283.0 = −110.5 kJ. −676.5 kJ adds without reversing, +110.5 kJ reverses the wrong equation, −221.0 kJ is for 2 mol of CO, and −393.5 kJ assumes CO forms as CO₂ does.

questions.stem: For CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, ΔH = −890 kJ. How much heat is released when 8.0 g of methane burns completely? (C 12.0, H 1.0)
questions.explain: Methane is 16.0 g/mol, so 8.0 g is 0.50 mol, and 0.50 × 890 = 445 kJ. 7,120 kJ multiplies by the grams, 890 kJ assumes one mole, 1,780 kJ divides 16 by 8 and multiplies, and 222.5 kJ halves again for the 2 in front of O₂, which doesn't apply to methane.

questions.stem: Bond energies: H-H 436 kJ/mol, Cl-Cl 243 kJ/mol, H-Cl 431 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl?
questions.explain: ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed = (436 + 243) − 2(431) = 679 − 862 = −183 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic. +183 kJ subtracts in the wrong order, +248 kJ forms only one H-Cl bond, −248 kJ forms one H-Cl bond and flips the sign, and −1,110 kJ adds all three bond energies.

questions.stem: How much energy is needed to melt 36.0 g of ice at 0 °C and then warm the water to 25.0 °C? (ΔHfus = 6.01 kJ/mol, water c = 4.18 J/(g·°C), H₂O 18.0 g/mol)
questions.explain: Melting: 36.0 ÷ 18.0 = 2.00 mol × 6.01 = 12.02 kJ. Warming: 36.0 × 4.18 × 25.0 = 3,762 J = 3.76 kJ. Total = 15.8 kJ. 12.0 kJ melts the ice but skips the warming, 3.76 kJ warms but skips melting, 220 kJ multiplies 6.01 by grams instead of moles, and 9.77 kJ uses 1 mol of ice for the melting step.

questions.stem: Nickel has Z = 28. Which is the ground-state electron configuration of the Ni²⁺ ion, and how many unpaired electrons does it have?
questions.explain: Neutral Ni is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁸ (28 electrons). Transition metals lose their 4s electrons first, so Ni²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁸ (26 electrons). By Hund's rule the five 3d orbitals each take one electron (5), then three pair up, leaving 5 − 3 = 2 unpaired. [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶ removes the 3d electrons first, 0 unpaired assumes an even electron count means everything is paired, 4s¹ 3d⁷ removes one electron from each subshell, and 8 unpaired ignores pairing once the five orbitals are half full.

questions.stem: Which lists the atoms F, Cl, Na, Mg and K in order of increasing atomic radius?
questions.explain: Radius grows down a group (more shells) and shrinks across a period (more protons pulling on the same shell). F is smaller than Cl (one shell fewer). In period 3, Cl (17 protons) < Mg (12) < Na (11). K starts a fourth shell, so it is largest: F < Cl < Mg < Na < K. The reverse list gives decreasing order, Na < Mg assumes more protons make a bigger atom, Cl < F has the group trend backwards, and placing Mg below Cl ignores the across-period shrink.

questions.stem: Which of these elements has the largest SECOND ionization energy: Na, Mg, Al, Si or K?
questions.explain: The second electron removed from Na comes out of the filled neon-like core (1s² 2s² 2p⁶), which is held very tightly, so Na's second ionization energy (about 4,560 kJ/mol) is far above the others. K's second electron also comes from a noble-gas core, but one shell farther out (about 3,050 kJ/mol). Mg's second electron is still a 3s valence electron (about 1,450), Si's is a 3p electron (about 1,580), and Al's comes from 3s (about 1,820). Picking Mg, Si or Al follows the first-ionization trend across the period, and picking K misses that its core is larger than sodium's.

questions.stem: In the best Lewis structure of the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻ (one C=O double bond and two C-O single bonds), how many lone pairs are there in total?
questions.explain: Valence electrons: 4 (C) + 3 × 6 (O) + 2 (charge) = 24. The bonds use 4 pairs (two single bonds and one double bond), or 8 electrons, leaving 16 electrons = 8 lone pairs (2 on the double-bonded O and 3 on each single-bonded O; carbon has none). 7 ignores the 2− charge (22 electrons), 9 draws only single bonds, 12 counts all 24 electrons as lone pairs, and 6 gives every oxygen just 2 lone pairs.

questions.stem: How many of these species are isoelectronic with argon: S²⁻, Cl⁻, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Na⁺, Br⁻ and Sc³⁺? (Z: Na 11, S 16, Cl 17, K 19, Ca 20, Sc 21, Br 35)
questions.explain: Argon has 18 electrons. Electrons = Z − charge: S²⁻ 16 + 2 = 18, Cl⁻ 18, K⁺ 18, Ca²⁺ 18, Na⁺ 10, Br⁻ 36, Sc³⁺ 21 − 3 = 18. Five species have 18 electrons. 4 misses Sc³⁺, 6 counts Br⁻ because it sits in the same group as Cl⁻, 7 counts every ion, and 3 counts only the cations K⁺, Ca²⁺ and Sc³⁺.

questions.stem: How many electrons in a ground-state sulfur atom (Z = 16) occupy p orbitals?
questions.explain: Sulfur is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. The p electrons are 2p⁶ + 3p⁴ = 10. 4 counts only the valence 3p electrons, 6 counts only the filled 2p subshell, 12 fills 3p completely, and 16 counts every electron in the atom.

questions.stem: What is the formula of iron(III) phosphate, and what is its molar mass? (Fe 55.8, P 31.0, O 16.0)
questions.explain: Iron(III) is Fe³⁺ and phosphate is PO₄³⁻, so the charges balance one to one: FePO₄. Molar mass = 55.8 + 31.0 + 4 × 16.0 = 150.8 g/mol. Fe₃(PO₄)₂ is iron(II) phosphate, Fe₂(PO₄)₃ crosses the Roman numeral and the ion charge without balancing them (+6 against −9), FePO₃ uses phosphite instead of phosphate, and Fe₃PO₄ balances the phosphate with three iron atoms as if each were +1.

questions.stem: Element X has successive ionization energies of 738, 1,451, 7,733 and 10,543 kJ/mol. What are the formulas of its chloride and its oxide?
questions.explain: The huge jump comes between the 2nd (1,451) and 3rd (7,733) ionization energies, so X has 2 valence electrons and forms X²⁺. With Cl⁻ that gives XCl₂, and with O²⁻ it gives XO. XCl and X₂O treat X as +1 (reading the first big step, 738 to 1,451, as the jump), XCl₃ and X₂O₃ count 3 electrons before the jump, XO₂ treats oxide as −1, and X₂Cl inverts the subscripts.

questions.stem: Heating 5.00 g of a magnesium sulfate hydrate, MgSO₄·xH₂O, drives off all the water and leaves 2.44 g of anhydrous MgSO₄. What is x? (Mg 24.3, S 32.1, O 16.0, H 1.0)
questions.explain: Water lost = 5.00 − 2.44 = 2.56 g = 2.56 ÷ 18.0 = 0.142 mol. MgSO₄ = 24.3 + 32.1 + 64.0 = 120.4 g/mol, so 2.44 g = 0.0203 mol. x = 0.142 ÷ 0.0203 = 7.0, MgSO₄·7H₂O. 1 compares the masses (2.56 ÷ 2.44) instead of moles, 3 divides by the whole 5.00 g as if it were all MgSO₄, 4 uses MgSO with only one oxygen (72.4 g/mol), and 8 uses 16 g/mol for water (oxygen only).

questions.stem: Complete combustion of 2.30 g of a compound containing only C, H and O gives 4.40 g of CO₂ and 2.70 g of H₂O. What is the compound's empirical formula? (C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0)
questions.explain: C: 4.40 ÷ 44.0 = 0.100 mol (1.20 g). H: 2.70 ÷ 18.0 = 0.150 mol H₂O, so 0.300 mol H (0.30 g). O by difference: 2.30 − 1.20 − 0.30 = 0.80 g = 0.050 mol. Ratio C : H : O = 0.100 : 0.300 : 0.050 = 2 : 6 : 1, so C₂H₆O. C₂H₃O forgets each H₂O has two H atoms, CH₃ forgets the oxygen in the compound, C₂H₆O₇ counts all the oxygen in the products (most came from the O₂), and C₄H₁₂O₂ doubles the ratio, which is a possible molecular formula, not the empirical one.

questions.stem: For 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O, 34.0 g of NH₃ reacts with 64.0 g of O₂. What is the maximum mass of NO that can form? (N 14.0, H 1.0, O 16.0)
questions.explain: NH₃: 34.0 ÷ 17.0 = 2.00 mol. O₂: 64.0 ÷ 32.0 = 2.00 mol. 2.00 mol NH₃ would need 2.00 × 5/4 = 2.50 mol O₂, so O₂ is limiting. NO = 2.00 × 4/5 = 1.60 mol × 30.0 = 48.0 g. 60.0 g treats NH₃ as limiting, 75.0 g inverts the O₂ : NO ratio (5/4), 96.0 g uses 16.0 g/mol for O₂ (atomic oxygen), and 98.0 g adds the reactant masses even though NO is only one of two products.

questions.stem: Iron is made by Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. A batch of 320 kg of Fe₂O₃ yields 168 kg of iron. What is the percent yield? (Fe 56.0, O 16.0)
questions.explain: Fe₂O₃ = 2 × 56.0 + 3 × 16.0 = 160 g/mol, so 320 kg = 2.00 kmol, which gives 4.00 kmol Fe = 224 kg in theory. Yield = 168 ÷ 224 = 75.0%. 150% forgets the 2 Fe per Fe₂O₃ (theoretical 112 kg), 52.5% divides the iron by the ore mass, 133% divides theoretical by actual, and 25.0% is the percent lost.

questions.stem: How many grams of sulfur are in 50.0 g of Al₂(SO₄)₃? (Al 27.0, S 32.1, O 16.0)
questions.explain: Molar mass = 2 × 27.0 + 3 × (32.1 + 64.0) = 342.3 g/mol, of which sulfur is 3 × 32.1 = 96.3 g. Mass of S = 50.0 × 96.3/342.3 = 14.1 g. 4.69 g counts only one sulfur atom, 13.0 g uses the formula AlSO₄, 42.1 g is the mass of all the sulfate, and 28.1 is the mass percent of sulfur, not a mass in 50.0 g.

questions.stem: How many hydrogen atoms are in 4.50 g of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆? (C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0, Avogadro's number 6.02 × 10²³)
questions.explain: Glucose = 180 g/mol, so 4.50 g = 0.0250 mol of molecules. Each has 12 H atoms: 0.0250 × 12 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.81 × 10²³. 1.51 × 10²² counts molecules, 9.03 × 10²² uses 6 H per molecule, 3.25 × 10²⁵ skips dividing by the molar mass, and 3.61 × 10²³ counts all 24 atoms.

questions.stem: What volume of 0.250 M AgNO₃ is needed to precipitate all the chloride from 1.11 g of CaCl₂ as AgCl? (Ca 40.0, Cl 35.5)
questions.explain: CaCl₂ = 111 g/mol, so 1.11 g = 0.0100 mol, which holds 0.0200 mol Cl⁻. Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl is 1 : 1, so 0.0200 mol Ag⁺ is needed: V = 0.0200 ÷ 0.250 = 0.0800 L = 80.0 mL. 40.0 mL forgets the 2 Cl⁻ per formula unit, 20.0 mL halves instead of doubling, 58.8 mL writes the salt as CaCl (75.5 g/mol), and 5.00 mL multiplies moles by molarity instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A metal M forms an oxide with the formula M₂O₃ that is 52.9% M by mass. What is the molar mass of M? (O 16.0)
questions.explain: In M₂O₃, 2M ÷ (2M + 48.0) = 0.529, so 2M = 0.529(2M + 48.0), 0.942M = 25.4 and M = 27.0 g/mol (aluminum). 18.0 uses the formula MO, 53.9 forgets the 2 on M, 21.4 uses 47.1% (the oxygen share) as the metal's share, and 9.0 counts only one oxygen (16.0) in the oxide.

questions.stem: Under the same conditions, a sample of an unknown gas takes 2.83 times as long to effuse as the same number of moles of helium. What is the molar mass of the unknown gas? (He 4.00)
questions.explain: Effusion rate ∝ 1/√M, so effusion time ∝ √M: t/t(He) = √(M/4.00). 2.83 = √(M/4.00), so M = 4.00 × 2.83² = 32.0 g/mol (O₂). 11.3 multiplies by 2.83 without squaring, 0.499 treats time like rate and divides, 6.73 multiplies by √2.83 instead of 2.83², and 8.01 squares 2.83 but forgets helium's molar mass.

questions.stem: A gas has a density of 2.86 g/L at 27 °C and 1.00 atm. What is its molar mass? (R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K))
questions.explain: From PV = nRT with n = m/M: M = dRT/P = 2.86 × 0.0821 × 300 ÷ 1.00 = 70.4 g/mol. 6.34 uses 27 instead of 300 K, 64.1 uses 273 K (STP) instead of the stated temperature, 0.116 inverts the expression (d/RT), and 7.13 × 10³ uses R = 8.314, which needs pascals and cubic meters, not atm and liters.

questions.stem: 250. mL of hydrogen is collected over water at 25 °C and a total pressure of 755 torr. The vapor pressure of water at 25 °C is 24 torr. How many moles of H₂ were collected? (R = 62.4 L·torr/(mol·K))
questions.explain: The gas is a mix of H₂ and water vapor, so P(H₂) = 755 − 24 = 731 torr. n = PV/RT = 731 × 0.250 ÷ (62.4 × 298) = 9.83 × 10⁻³ mol. 1.02 × 10⁻² uses the total pressure, 1.05 × 10⁻² adds the vapor pressure instead of subtracting it, 1.17 × 10⁻¹ uses 25 instead of 298 K, and 9.83 mol leaves the volume in milliliters.

questions.stem: An airbag inflates by 2NaN₃ → 2Na + 3N₂. What mass of NaN₃ is needed to make 65.0 L of N₂ at 25 °C and 1.10 atm? (Na 23.0, N 14.0, R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K))
questions.explain: n(N₂) = PV/RT = 1.10 × 65.0 ÷ (0.0821 × 298) = 2.92 mol. NaN₃ = 2.92 × 2/3 = 1.95 mol × 65.0 g/mol = 127 g. 190 g uses a 1 : 1 ratio, 285 g inverts the ratio (3/2), 1,510 g uses 25 instead of 298 K, and 115 g leaves out the 1.10 atm pressure.

questions.stem: A tire gauge reads 32.0 psi at 10 °C. After a drive the air inside is at 45 °C, with the tire volume unchanged. What does the gauge read now? (atmospheric pressure = 14.7 psi; the gauge shows pressure above atmospheric)
questions.explain: Gas laws need absolute pressure and kelvin. P₁ = 32.0 + 14.7 = 46.7 psi at 283 K. P₂ = 46.7 × 318/283 = 52.5 psi absolute, so the gauge reads 52.5 − 14.7 = 37.8 psi. 36.0 psi scales the gauge reading directly, 144 psi uses Celsius temperatures, 52.5 psi forgets to convert back to gauge pressure, and 26.9 psi inverts the temperature ratio.

questions.stem: A 2.00 L flask of N₂ at 3.00 atm is connected by a valve to a 3.00 L flask of O₂ at 1.50 atm. The valve is opened and the gases mix at constant temperature. What is the final total pressure?
questions.explain: Each gas spreads into the full 5.00 L (Boyle's law). P(N₂) = 3.00 × 2.00/5.00 = 1.20 atm, P(O₂) = 1.50 × 3.00/5.00 = 0.900 atm, so the total is 2.10 atm. 4.50 atm adds the starting pressures, 2.25 atm averages them, 1.20 atm is only the N₂ partial pressure, and 2.40 atm swaps the two flask volumes.

questions.stem: At constant temperature and pressure, 6.0 L of H₂ and 4.0 L of N₂ react as completely as possible by N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. What is the total volume of gas afterwards?
questions.explain: Gas volumes react in mole ratios. 6.0 L H₂ needs only 2.0 L N₂, so H₂ is limiting. It makes 6.0 × 2/3 = 4.0 L NH₃, and 4.0 − 2.0 = 2.0 L N₂ is left over: total 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 L. 4.0 L counts only the NH₃, 10.0 L assumes the volume doesn't change, 8.0 L treats N₂ as limiting (8.0 L NH₃), and 2.0 L counts only the leftover N₂.

questions.stem: A buffer is 0.20 M acetic acid and 0.30 M sodium acetate. Acetic acid's Ka is 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. What is the pH of the buffer?
questions.explain: Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). pKa = −log(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.74, and log(0.30/0.20) = 0.18, so pH = 4.92. 4.57 inverts the ratio (acid over base), 4.74 is the pKa alone (equal amounts), 2.72 treats the solution as acetic acid only and ignores the acetate, and 5.15 uses the natural log of the ratio.

questions.stem: 50.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl is mixed with 30.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. What is the pH of the mixture?
questions.explain: H⁺: 0.0500 × 0.100 = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol. OH⁻: 0.0300 × 0.100 = 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol. After neutralization 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol H⁺ remains in 80.0 mL: [H⁺] = 0.0250 M, pH = 1.60. 1.40 divides by the acid's 50.0 mL only, 1.00 ignores the base, 12.40 reports 14 − pH (the pOH confusion), and 1.18 divides by the base's 30.0 mL.

questions.stem: A 0.050 M solution of a weak monoprotic acid HA has a pH of 3.00. What is Ka for HA?
questions.explain: [H⁺] = [A⁻] = 10^(−3.00) = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M, and [HA] ≈ 0.050 − 0.001 = 0.049 M. Ka = (1.0 × 10⁻³)² ÷ 0.049 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵. 2.0 × 10⁻² sets Ka = [H⁺]/[HA] without squaring, 1.0 × 10⁻³ reports [H⁺] itself, 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ is the numerator without dividing by [HA], and 5.0 × 10⁻⁸ multiplies by [HA] instead of dividing.

questions.stem: What volume of 0.150 M NaOH is needed to neutralize all three acidic protons in 20.0 mL of 0.225 M H₃PO₄?
questions.explain: H₃PO₄: 0.0200 × 0.225 = 4.50 × 10⁻³ mol, which supplies 3 × 4.50 × 10⁻³ = 0.0135 mol H⁺. V(NaOH) = 0.0135 ÷ 0.150 = 0.0900 L = 90.0 mL. 30.0 mL uses a 1 : 1 ratio, 60.0 mL counts only two protons, 40.0 mL swaps the two molarities in M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ before tripling, and 10.0 mL divides by 3 instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: 10.0 mL of a 2.00 M stock solution is diluted to 250. mL. Then 5.00 mL of that solution is diluted to 100. mL. What is the final concentration?
questions.explain: First dilution: 2.00 × 10.0/250. = 0.0800 M. Second: 0.0800 × 5.00/100. = 4.00 × 10⁻³ M. 8.00 × 10⁻² M stops after the first step, 3.66 × 10⁻³ M adds 250 mL and 100 mL of water to the aliquots instead of making them up to those volumes, 1.60 M inverts the second ratio, and 1.00 × 10⁻¹ M applies the second dilution to the stock.

questions.stem: 11.7 g of NaCl is dissolved in 500. g of water. Taking Kf = 1.86 °C·kg/mol and full dissociation, what is the freezing point of the solution? (Na 23.0, Cl 35.5)
questions.explain: NaCl: 11.7 ÷ 58.5 = 0.200 mol in 0.500 kg of water, molality 0.400 m. NaCl gives 2 ions (i = 2): ΔTf = 2 × 1.86 × 0.400 = 1.49 °C, so it freezes at −1.49 °C. −0.744 °C ignores the dissociation, −1.45 °C divides by the solution mass (511.7 g) instead of the solvent mass, −2.23 °C uses i = 3, and −0.00149 °C leaves the water in grams.

questions.stem: Concentrated sulfuric acid is 96.0% H₂SO₄ by mass and has a density of 1.84 g/mL. What is its molarity? (H 1.0, S 32.1, O 16.0)
questions.explain: One liter weighs 1,840 g, of which 96.0% (1,766 g) is H₂SO₄. H₂SO₄ = 98.1 g/mol, so 1,766 ÷ 98.1 = 18.0 mol per liter. 18.8 M treats the acid as 100% pure, 18.4 M uses the molar mass of SO₄ (96.1), 0.0180 M uses the density per liter instead of per milliliter, and 36.0 M doubles for the two protons, which is the normality, not the molarity.

questions.stem: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, a 2.00 L vessel at equilibrium holds 0.400 mol N₂, 1.20 mol H₂ and 0.800 mol NH₃. What is Kc?
questions.explain: Concentrations: [N₂] = 0.200 M, [H₂] = 0.600 M, [NH₃] = 0.400 M. Kc = [NH₃]² ÷ ([N₂][H₂]³) = 0.160 ÷ (0.200 × 0.216) = 3.70. 0.926 plugs in moles instead of molarities, 3.33 ignores the coefficients as exponents, 0.270 inverts the expression (reactants over products), and 2.22 multiplies by the coefficients instead of raising to them.

questions.stem: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), Kc = 64 at a certain temperature. 1.00 mol of H₂ and 1.00 mol of I₂ are sealed in a 1.00 L flask and reach equilibrium. What is the equilibrium concentration of HI?
questions.explain: Let x react: [H₂] = [I₂] = 1.00 − x and [HI] = 2x. Kc = (2x)² ÷ (1.00 − x)² = 64, so 2x/(1.00 − x) = 8, giving 2x = 8 − 8x and x = 0.800. [HI] = 2x = 1.60 M. 0.889 M forgets the 2 in front of HI, 8.00 M ignores the reactants being used up, 0.800 M reports x instead of 2x, and 0.200 M is the H₂ left at equilibrium.

questions.stem: For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, Kc = 280 at a certain temperature. A 1.00 L vessel contains 0.500 mol SO₂, 0.100 mol O₂ and 2.00 mol SO₃. Which describes the system?
options: Q = 160, so it shifts right to make SO₃
Q = 160, so it shifts left to make SO₂
Q = 40, so it shifts right to make SO₃
Q = 280, so it is already at equilibrium
questions.explain: Q = [SO₃]² ÷ ([SO₂]²[O₂]) = 2.00² ÷ (0.500² × 0.100) = 4.00 ÷ 0.0250 = 160. Q < K, so the reaction runs forward (right) until Q rises to 280. Shifting left reverses the Q < K rule, Q = 40 ignores the squares, 6.25 × 10⁻³ inverts the expression, and the equilibrium choice assumes any mixture already sits at K.

questions.stem: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), ΔH = +57 kJ. Which change increases the amount of NO₂ present at equilibrium?
options: Raising the temperature at constant volume
Shrinking the volume at constant temperature
Adding a catalyst at constant temperature
Lowering the temperature at constant volume
questions.explain: The forward reaction is endothermic, so heating favors it and makes more NO₂. Shrinking the volume raises pressure and favors the side with fewer gas moles (1 mol N₂O₄ against 2 mol NO₂), so it lowers NO₂. A catalyst speeds both directions equally and doesn't move the equilibrium, argon at constant volume changes no partial pressures, and cooling favors the exothermic reverse reaction.

questions.stem: The Ksp of calcium fluoride, CaF₂, is 3.9 × 10⁻¹¹. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
questions.explain: CaF₂ ⇌ Ca²⁺ + 2F⁻. If s mol/L dissolve, [Ca²⁺] = s and [F⁻] = 2s, so Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³. s = ∛(3.9 × 10⁻¹¹ ÷ 4) = 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ M. 6.2 × 10⁻⁶ M takes √Ksp as for a 1 : 1 salt, 3.4 × 10⁻⁴ M forgets to square the 2 (∛Ksp), 9.8 × 10⁻¹² M divides by 4 but never takes the root, and 4.4 × 10⁻⁶ M writes Ksp = s × 2s.

questions.stem: The Ksp of silver chloride is 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. What is the molar solubility of AgCl in 0.10 M NaCl?
questions.explain: The NaCl fixes [Cl⁻] at 0.10 M, and the small amount of AgCl that dissolves (s) barely changes it. Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = s × 0.10, so s = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M. 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M is the solubility in pure water (√Ksp), 4.2 × 10⁻⁵ M takes √(Ksp ÷ 0.10), 1.8 × 10⁻¹¹ M multiplies by 0.10 instead of dividing, and 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ M takes Ksp as the solubility.

questions.stem: Ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, contains two nitrogen atoms in different environments. What are their oxidation numbers?
questions.explain: Split the salt into its ions. In NH₄⁺: N + 4(+1) = +1, so N = −3. In NO₃⁻: N + 3(−2) = −1, so N = +5. +1 and +1 averages the two nitrogens over the whole formula ((−3 + 5) ÷ 2), +5 and +5 gives hydrogen −1 in NH₄⁺, +6 ignores the nitrate's −1 charge, and −4 ignores the ammonium's +1 charge.

questions.stem: When Cr₂O₇²⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Cr³⁺ + Fe³⁺ is balanced in acidic solution, how many Fe²⁺ ions and how many H⁺ ions react with each dichromate ion?
questions.explain: Each Cr goes from +6 to +3, gaining 3 electrons, and dichromate has 2 Cr, so it gains 6 electrons: 6 Fe²⁺ each lose 1. The 7 O atoms become 7 H₂O, which needs 14 H⁺: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O (charge 24+ on each side). 3 Fe²⁺ counts only one Cr, 7 H⁺ matches H⁺ to the oxygen count, 12 Fe²⁺ takes Cr all the way to 0, and 8 H⁺ copies the permanganate equation.

questions.stem: A current of 2.50 A passes through a CuSO₄ solution for 30.0 minutes. What mass of copper plates out at the cathode? (Cu 63.5, F = 96,500 C/mol)
questions.explain: Charge Q = It = 2.50 × 1,800 s = 4,500 C = 4,500 ÷ 96,500 = 0.0466 mol of electrons. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so 0.0233 mol Cu × 63.5 = 1.48 g. 2.96 g forgets the 2 electrons per Cu²⁺, 0.0247 g leaves the time in minutes, 3.72 g uses the molar mass of CuSO₄, and 4.11 × 10⁻⁴ g uses the time in hours.

questions.stem: Standard reduction potentials: Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V and Ag⁺/Ag = +0.80 V. What is the standard cell potential of Zn + 2Ag⁺ → Zn²⁺ + 2Ag?
questions.explain: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V. Silver is reduced (cathode) and zinc oxidized (anode). Potentials are intensive, so the coefficient 2 on Ag does not double 0.80 V. 2.36 V doubles the silver potential, 0.04 V adds the two signed values, −1.56 V subtracts the wrong way round, and 0.84 V doubles silver and then subtracts zinc's magnitude.

questions.stem: Radium-226 (Z = 88) emits an alpha particle, and its daughter then emits a second alpha particle. What nucleus results?
questions.explain: Each alpha particle (⁴He, Z = 2) lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. Two alphas: A = 226 − 8 = 218 and Z = 88 − 4 = 84, which is polonium: ²¹⁸Po. ²²²Rn stops after one decay, ²¹⁸Rn lowers A for both decays but Z for only one, ²²²Po swaps the changes (A down 4 in total, Z down 4), and ²¹⁸Ra lowers the mass number but leaves Z unchanged.

questions.stem: In a reactor, a cobalt-59 nucleus (Z = 27) absorbs a neutron, and the product later undergoes beta-minus decay. What nucleus is formed at the end?
questions.explain: Neutron capture adds 1 to A only: ⁵⁹Co + ¹n → ⁶⁰Co. Beta-minus decay turns a neutron into a proton, so Z rises by 1 and A stays 60: ⁶⁰Co → ⁶⁰Ni + β⁻. ⁶⁰Co stops after the capture, ⁵⁹Ni forgets the neutron's mass, ⁶⁰Fe lowers Z for beta-minus (that's positron emission), and ⁶¹Ni adds a mass unit for the beta particle too.

questions.stem: Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8.02 days. What is the activity of a 1.00 µg sample of pure iodine-131? (I-131 = 131 g/mol, Avogadro's number 6.02 × 10²³, 1 Bq = 1 decay per second)
questions.explain: Nuclei: N = (1.00 × 10⁻⁶ g ÷ 131) × 6.02 × 10²³ = 4.60 × 10¹⁵. Decay constant: λ = ln 2 ÷ t½ = 0.693 ÷ (8.02 × 86,400 s) = 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹. Activity = λN = 4.60 × 10⁹ Bq. 6.63 × 10⁹ uses λ = 1/t½ without ln 2, 3.97 × 10¹⁴ leaves the half-life in days (decays per day, not per second), 4.60 × 10¹² treats µg as mg, and 4.60 × 10¹⁵ is the number of nuclei, not the decay rate.

questions.stem: An iron-56 nucleus (26 protons, 30 neutrons) has a mass of 55.92068 u. A proton is 1.00728 u and a neutron is 1.00866 u. What is its binding energy per nucleon? (1 u = 931.5 MeV)
questions.explain: Separate nucleons: 26 × 1.00728 + 30 × 1.00866 = 56.44908 u. Mass defect = 56.44908 − 55.92068 = 0.52840 u, so the binding energy is 0.52840 × 931.5 = 492 MeV, and per nucleon 492 ÷ 56 = 8.79 MeV. 492 MeV is the total, 18.9 MeV divides by the 26 protons only, 16.4 MeV divides by the 30 neutrons only, and 8.55 MeV uses the neutral-atom mass (55.93494 u) against bare protons.

questions.stem: A reactor runs at 3,000 MW of thermal power. Each U-235 fission releases 200 MeV. What mass of U-235 fissions in one day? (1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J, Avogadro's number 6.02 × 10²³, U-235 = 235 g/mol)
questions.explain: Energy per fission = 200 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 3.20 × 10⁻¹¹ J. Fissions per second = 3.00 × 10⁹ W ÷ 3.20 × 10⁻¹¹ J = 9.38 × 10¹⁹; per day × 86,400 = 8.10 × 10²⁴ fissions = 13.5 mol × 235 g/mol = 3,160 g = 3.16 kg. 0.132 kg is one hour's worth, 0.00316 kg treats MW as kW, 0.00288 kg converts the whole mass to energy with E = mc² (fission converts only about 0.1% of it), and 3.16 × 10³ kg reads grams as kilograms.

questions.stem: A gamma source gives 800 mR/h at 1.0 m with no shielding. A worker adds lead three half-value layers thick and moves back to 2.0 m. What is the new dose rate?
questions.explain: Three half-value layers cut the intensity by 2³ = 8: 800 ÷ 8 = 100 mR/h at 1.0 m. Doubling the distance from a point source cuts it by 2² = 4 (inverse square): 100 ÷ 4 = 25 mR/h. 50 mR/h treats distance as a straight 1/d, 100 mR/h ignores the move, 200 mR/h ignores the lead, and 33.3 mR/h treats three half-value layers as dividing by 2 × 3 = 6.

questions.stem: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO, ΔH = +180.6 kJ. 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, ΔH = −114.2 kJ. What is ΔH for NO₂ → ½N₂ + O₂?
questions.explain: Adding the two equations gives N₂ + 2O₂ → 2NO₂, ΔH = 180.6 − 114.2 = +66.4 kJ. The target is that reaction reversed and halved: ΔH = −66.4 ÷ 2 = −33.2 kJ. +33.2 kJ halves but forgets to reverse the sign, −66.4 kJ reverses but forgets to halve, −147.4 kJ subtracts the second ΔH instead of adding it (180.6 + 114.2) before reversing and halving, and +147.4 kJ makes that slip and also skips the reversal.

questions.stem: Average bond energies: C-H 413, O=O 498, C=O 799 and O-H 463 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O?
questions.explain: Bonds broken: 4 C-H + 2 O=O = 4(413) + 2(498) = 2,648 kJ. Bonds formed: 2 C=O + 4 O-H = 2(799) + 4(463) = 3,450 kJ. ΔH = broken − formed = 2,648 − 3,450 = −802 kJ. +802 kJ subtracts the wrong way round, −1,300 kJ breaks only one O=O, +124 kJ counts only one O-H per water, and −6,098 kJ adds the two totals.

questions.stem: Dissolving 4.00 g of NaOH in 100.0 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter raises the temperature from 20.0 °C to 30.4 °C. Taking the solution's specific heat as 4.18 J/(g·°C), what is ΔH of solution in kJ per mole of NaOH? (Na 23.0, O 16.0, H 1.0)
questions.explain: q = mcΔT = 104.0 g × 4.18 × 10.4 °C = 4,521 J absorbed by the solution, so the dissolving released 4.52 kJ. NaOH: 4.00 ÷ 40.0 = 0.100 mol, so ΔH = −4.52 ÷ 0.100 = −45.2 kJ/mol. −43.5 uses only the 100.0 g of water, +45.2 misses that a temperature rise means an exothermic process, −4.52 forgets to divide by moles, and −132 uses the final temperature (30.4 °C) as ΔT.
